lessons.title: 9.1 Reversible Reactions and Dynamic Equilibrium
lessons.notes_html:
Equilibrium is a Latin word meaning balance of forces. It is the state when there seems no change in a system, e.g. a pencil kept on a finger at rest.

Two Types of Equilibrium

  • Static equilibrium: the different phases remain at rest, e.g. the fulcrum and the playground seesaw.
  • Dynamic equilibrium: the phases readily interconvert, e.g. in vapour pressure the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation, so net change is zero.

Water, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and ozone cycles exist in dynamic equilibrium.

Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions are reversible: products can be transformed back into reactants. General form: A + B <=> C + D. The double-headed half arrow shows change in both directions. Chemical equilibrium is where the rate of producing C and D equals the rate of reproducing A and B.

  • Ammonia: 3H2(g) + N2(g) <=> 2NH3(g). NH3 can again give H2 and N2; NH3 is an important constituent of urea fertilizer.
  • N2O4(l) <=> 2NO2(g) at 140C: N2O4 is pale yellow (liquid), NO2 is reddish brown (gas).
  • H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g): colourless H2 + purple I2 form colourless HI, which decomposes back.
  • Sulphur trioxide: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g).

In the H2 + I2 graph, H2 and I2 concentrations fall and HI rises, then all become constant. At equilibrium all three species are present, the reaction does not stop, and rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction. All reactions are reversible, but the extent of reversibility varies greatly.

Key Points

  • Equilibrium means balance of forces and no apparent change in the system.
  • Static equilibrium is at rest; dynamic equilibrium has equal opposite changes and zero net change.
  • A reversible reaction is written with <=>, e.g. 3H2 + N2 <=> 2NH3.
  • At dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant.
  • The reaction does not stop at equilibrium; all species remain present.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'equilibrium' literally mean?
options: Balance of forces, a state in which there seems to be no change in the system
Complete stoppage of all reactions in the system
A state in which only the forward reaction takes place
A state in which products can never change back into reactants
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is a Latin word meaning balance of forces. It is the state when there seems no change in a system, like a pencil kept balanced on a finger at rest.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of static equilibrium?
options: Evaporation and condensation taking place at equal rates in a closed vessel
A pencil balanced on a finger, or the fulcrum and playground seesaw at rest
The nitrogen cycle running continuously in nature
Ammonia continuously forming and decomposing in a reactor
mcqs.why: In static equilibrium the different phases remain at rest, as with a pencil on a finger or a seesaw fulcrum. Evaporation-condensation and the natural cycles are dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In dynamic equilibrium, such as vapour pressure over a liquid, what is true?
options: Evaporation stops completely once equilibrium is reached
The rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation, so the net change is zero
All the liquid is converted into vapour
mcqs.why: Dynamic equilibrium means the phases readily interconvert: evaporation and condensation continue at equal rates, so there is no net change in the system.

mcqs.q: How is a reversible reaction written?
options: With a single arrow pointing only towards the products
With an equals sign between reactants and products
With a cross mark between reactants and products
With a double-headed half arrow, e.g. A + B <=> C + D
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction, in which products can change back into reactants, is written with the <=> sign, e.g. A + B <=> C + D.

mcqs.q: What is the correct equation for the synthesis of ammonia?
mcqs.why: Ammonia is formed reversibly as 3H2(g) + N2(g) <=> 2NH3(g): one molecule of nitrogen reacts with three molecules of hydrogen to give two molecules of ammonia, and NH3 can decompose back.

mcqs.q: At chemical equilibrium in the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g), what happens to the concentrations?
options: The concentrations of H2 and I2 fall to zero
The concentrations of H2, I2 and HI all become constant, although the reaction does not stop
Only HI remains present in the vessel
The concentration of HI keeps on increasing slowly
mcqs.why: In the H2 + I2 graph, H2 and I2 fall and HI rises until all become constant. At equilibrium all three species are present, the reaction does not stop, and forward rate equals reverse rate.

mcqs.q: In the equilibrium N2O4(l) <=> 2NO2(g) at 140 C, what are the colours of the two substances?
options: N2O4 is colourless and NO2 is pale yellow
N2O4 is reddish brown and NO2 is pale yellow
N2O4 is pale yellow (liquid) and NO2 is reddish brown (gas)
Both N2O4 and NO2 are colourless
mcqs.why: The notes state that in N2O4(l) <=> 2NO2(g), N2O4 is a pale yellow liquid while the product NO2 is a reddish brown gas.

mcqs.q: In the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g), which substance is purple in colour?
mcqs.why: Colourless H2 and purple I2 form colourless HI, which can decompose back into H2 and I2. Only iodine is purple.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a reaction at dynamic equilibrium is correct?
options: The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction
The forward reaction continues but the reverse reaction stops
The amounts of reactants and products must be exactly equal
mcqs.why: Chemical equilibrium is where the rate of producing C and D equals the rate of reproducing A and B. The reaction does not stop; only the two rates become equal.

mcqs.q: Why is ammonia, NH3, industrially important according to this lesson?
options: It is used as a fuel in rockets
It is an important constituent of urea fertilizer
It is used for filling balloons
It is used in the manufacture of glass
mcqs.why: The notes point out that NH3 formed in the reversible reaction N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 is an important constituent of urea fertilizer.

lessons.title: 9.2 Law of Mass Action and Derivation of the Expression for the Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
In 1864 two scientists, Guldberg and Waage, studied the relation of dynamic equilibrium with quantities or concentration and put forward the law of mass action.

Law of Mass Action

The rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of active masses (or concentration) of reactants at constant temperature.

Derivation for A + B <=> C + D

  • Forward reaction: A + B -> C + D
  • Reverse reaction: C + D -> A + B
  • Rate of forward reaction Rf = Kf [A] [B]
  • Rate of reverse reaction Rr = Kr [C] [D]

Here [ ] shows molar concentration and Kf, Kr are proportionality constants.

At dynamic equilibrium the rates are equal: Rf = Rr, so Kf [A] [B] = Kr [C] [D]. Rearranging: Kf / Kr = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]). As Kf and Kr are both constants, Kf / Kr = Kc, the equilibrium constant.

Therefore: Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B])

General Form and Kp

For aA + bB <=> cC + dD: Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where a, b, c and d are the reaction coefficients, written as powers.

In gaseous systems, partial pressure of gases is taken instead of concentration, so Kp is used instead of Kc. For aA(g) + bB(g) <=> cC(g) + dD(g): Kp = (pC)^c (pD)^d / ((pA)^a (pB)^b), where p is the partial pressure of a gas.

Key Points

  • Law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in 1864.
  • Rate is directly proportional to the product of active masses of reactants at constant temperature.
  • At equilibrium Rf = Rr, which gives Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]).
  • In the general expression, each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.
  • For gases, Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations.

mcqs.q: The law of mass action was put forward in 1864 by:
mcqs.why: In 1864 two scientists, Guldberg and Waage, studied the relation of dynamic equilibrium with quantities or concentration and put forward the law of mass action.

mcqs.q: According to the law of mass action, the rate of a chemical reaction is:
options: Inversely proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants
Directly proportional to the sum of the concentrations of the products
Directly proportional to the product of the active masses (concentrations) of the reactants at constant temperature
Independent of the concentrations of the reactants
mcqs.why: The law of mass action states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of active masses, or concentrations, of reactants at constant temperature.

mcqs.q: In the rate expressions Rf = Kf [A] [B], the square brackets [ ] show:
mcqs.why: In the derivation, [ ] shows molar concentration, while Kf and Kr are the proportionality constants for the forward and reverse reactions.

mcqs.q: For the reaction A + B <=> C + D, the rate of the forward reaction is:
mcqs.why: The forward reaction A + B -> C + D has rate Rf = Kf [A] [B]; the reverse reaction C + D -> A + B has rate Rr = Kr [C] [D].

mcqs.q: At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse rates are related as:
mcqs.why: At dynamic equilibrium the rates are equal: Rf = Rr, which gives Kf [A] [B] = Kr [C] [D], and rearranging this gives the equilibrium constant expression.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant for A + B <=> C + D is:
mcqs.why: From Kf [A] [B] = Kr [C] [D] we get Kf / Kr = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]). Since Kf and Kr are constants, Kf / Kr = Kc, so Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]).

mcqs.q: For A + B <=> C + D, if [A] = 0.2, [B] = 0.2, [C] = 0.4 and [D] = 0.4 mol dm-3, the value of Kc is:
mcqs.why: Working: Kc = [C] [D] / ([A] [B]) = (0.4 x 0.4) / (0.2 x 0.2) = 0.16 / 0.04 = 4. The units cancel here because the same number of concentration terms appears above and below.

mcqs.q: In the general expression Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b) for aA + bB <=> cC + dD, the letters a, b, c and d are:
options: The reaction coefficients, and each concentration is raised to the power of its own coefficient
The atomic numbers of the elements taking part
The temperatures at which the reaction is carried out
The volumes of the gases used
mcqs.why: In the general form, a, b, c and d are the coefficients of the balanced equation, and each concentration is written raised to the power of its coefficient.

mcqs.q: For a gaseous equilibrium, the constant Kp is used instead of Kc because:
options: Partial pressures of the gases are taken instead of their concentrations
The temperature of gases cannot be measured
Gases do not obey the law of mass action
mcqs.why: In gaseous systems, partial pressure of gases is taken instead of concentration, so Kp = (pC)^c (pD)^d / ((pA)^a (pB)^b) is used instead of Kc.

mcqs.q: In the derivation of Kc, the ratio Kf / Kr is equal to Kc because:
options: Kf and Kr are both equal to one
Kf and Kr cancel each other out
Both Kf and Kr are constants, so their ratio is also a constant
Kf and Kr are the concentrations of the reactants
mcqs.why: Kf and Kr are both proportionality constants, so Kf / Kr is itself a constant, and this constant ratio is defined as the equilibrium constant Kc.

lessons.title: 9.3 Equilibrium Constant and Its Units
lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant Kc tells us the concentration of different species of the reaction at both the reactant and product sides at the time of equilibrium.

Kc = Product of the concentration of products raised to the power of coefficient / Product of the concentration of reactants raised to the power of coefficient.

It helps in calculating the concentration of species of a reaction, and with suitable applications we can enhance the quantity of the desired species of a reversible reaction.

What Kc Depends On

  • Kc depends upon temperature: if temperature is changed, its value also changes.
  • Kc does not depend upon the initial concentration of reactants or products.

Units of Kc

Kc is a ratio, so units may cancel. Its units vary from case to case.

ReactionKc ExpressionUnits
H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g) at 450CKc = [HI]^2 / ([H2] [I2])No units: (mol dm-3)^2 / ((mol dm-3)(mol dm-3)) cancel
N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) at 450CKc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3)(mol dm-3)^-2, because moles of reactants and products are not equal

So: when the number of moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no units; when they are not equal, Kc has units.

Key Points

  • Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient.
  • Kc changes only with temperature, not with initial concentrations.
  • For H2 + I2 <=> 2HI, Kc has no units.
  • For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kc has units (mol dm-3)^-2.
  • Units of Kc vary from case to case.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant Kc depends upon:
options: The initial concentration of the reactants
The initial concentration of the products
Temperature only; it does not depend on the initial concentrations of reactants or products
The size of the reaction vessel
mcqs.why: Kc depends upon temperature: if temperature is changed, its value also changes. It does not depend upon the initial concentration of reactants or products.

mcqs.q: For the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g) at 450 C, Kc has no units because:
options: Hydrogen and iodine are both gases
The reaction is carried out at a very high temperature
The number of moles of reactants and products is equal, so the (mol dm-3) terms cancel out
mcqs.why: Kc = [HI]^2 / ([H2] [I2]); the units are (mol dm-3)^2 / ((mol dm-3)(mol dm-3)), which cancel. When moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no units.

mcqs.q: The units of Kc for N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) are:
mcqs.why: Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] [H2]^3). The powers give (mol dm-3)^2 / (mol dm-3)^4 = (mol dm-3)^-2, because the moles of reactants (4) and products (2) are not equal.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium for N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, [NH3] = 0.4, [N2] = 0.2 and [H2] = 0.4 mol dm-3. Kc is:
Why do the units of Kc vary from case to case?
options: Because different thermometers are used in different experiments
Because Kc is measured in different countries
Because Kc is a ratio of concentrations, and the units cancel only when the total moles of reactants and products are equal
Because the units depend on the colour of the products
mcqs.why: Kc is a ratio, so its units may cancel. When the number of moles of reactants and products are equal the units cancel; when they are not equal, Kc keeps units such as (mol dm-3)^-2.

mcqs.q: One use of the equilibrium constant Kc is:
options: To measure the temperature of a reaction mixture
To weigh the products of a reaction
To change the colour of the products
To calculate the concentration of the species of a reaction at equilibrium
mcqs.why: Kc tells us the concentrations of the different species on the reactant and product sides at equilibrium, and it helps in calculating the concentration of species of a reaction.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of an equilibrium reaction is changed, what happens to Kc?
options: It becomes equal to the initial concentration
mcqs.why: Kc depends upon temperature: if temperature is changed, its value also changes. This is the only factor among those listed that changes Kc.

mcqs.q: The correct Kc expression for H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g) is:
mcqs.why: Products go on top raised to their coefficients and reactants below: for H2 + I2 <=> 2HI, Kc = [HI]^2 / ([H2] [I2]), and its units cancel completely.

mcqs.q: In the Kc expression, each concentration is raised to the power of:
options: The coefficient of that species in the balanced equation
mcqs.why: Kc is the product of the concentrations of products raised to the power of their coefficients, divided by the product of the concentrations of reactants raised to the power of their coefficients.

mcqs.q: With suitable applications of Kc, we can:
options: Convert an irreversible reaction into a reversible one
Remove the need for a catalyst in every reaction
Enhance the quantity of the desired species of a reversible reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state that Kc helps in calculating concentrations, and with suitable applications we can enhance the quantity of the desired species of a reversible reaction.

lessons.title: 9.4 Importance of Equilibrium Constant
lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant has many applications in chemistry. The value of Kc is used to calculate important phenomena of reversible reactions used in industries.

Industrial Use

Kc is used to calculate the amount of reactants or products of reversible reactions of industrially important compounds like sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3), urea CO(NH2)2.

Increasing the Yield of Ammonia

For NH3, used in synthesis of urea fertilizer: N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) at 450C, and Kp = (NH3)^2 / ((N2) (H2)^3). Kp has a constant value, so to increase NH3:

  • Increase the concentration / pressure of N2.
  • Increase the concentration / pressure of H2.
  • Decrease the amount of NH3 by removal.

Then more NH3 is formed and hence more urea can be formed.

Predicting Direction and Extent

  • Kc is used to predict the direction of a chemical reaction and, after a specific time, its extent.
  • Very high Kc: concentration of products is very high at equilibrium, so the desired product can be easily made.
  • Very low Kc: concentration of initial reactants is high at equilibrium, so the reaction is not feasible.
  • Kc helps calculate the effect of changing conditions, so the yield can be controlled; this decreases expenditure of preparation and product prices can be controlled to a desired level.

Key Points

  • Kc is used in industry for H2SO4, HNO3 and urea manufacture.
  • More NH3 is obtained by increasing N2 or H2 and by removing NH3.
  • High Kc means products dominate and the reaction is feasible.
  • Low Kc means reactants dominate and the reaction is not feasible.
  • Kc predicts direction and extent and helps control yield.

mcqs.q: Kc is used in industry to calculate the amounts of reactants or products for compounds such as:
options: Hydrochloric acid, common salt and washing soda only
Sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3) and urea CO(NH2)2
mcqs.why: The value of Kc is used to calculate important phenomena of reversible reactions used in industries, for industrially important compounds like sulphuric acid, nitric acid and urea.

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), the yield of ammonia can be increased by:
options: Increasing the concentration or pressure of N2 and H2, and removing NH3 as it is formed
Decreasing the pressure of nitrogen and hydrogen
Adding more and more ammonia to the mixture
Cooling the mixture to room temperature and sealing it
mcqs.why: Kp has a constant value, so to increase NH3 we increase the concentration/pressure of N2, increase the concentration/pressure of H2, and decrease the amount of NH3 by removing it; then more NH3, and hence more urea, is formed.

mcqs.q: Removing ammonia from the equilibrium mixture as it forms results in:
options: More ammonia being formed to restore the balance
All the nitrogen changing into hydrogen
The value of Kp becoming zero
mcqs.why: Decreasing the amount of NH3 by removal disturbs the equilibrium, so the forward reaction produces more NH3. This is how the yield of ammonia, and hence of urea fertilizer, is increased.

mcqs.q: A very high value of Kc means:
options: The concentration of reactants is very high at equilibrium
The reaction cannot take place at all
The concentration of products is very high at equilibrium, so the desired product can be easily made
mcqs.why: Very high Kc means the concentration of products is very high at equilibrium, so the desired product can be easily made and the reaction is feasible.

mcqs.q: A very low value of Kc means:
options: The products are formed very quickly and completely
The concentration of the initial reactants is high at equilibrium, so the reaction is not feasible
mcqs.why: Very low Kc means the concentration of initial reactants is high at equilibrium, so very little product forms and the reaction is not feasible.

mcqs.q: Apart from extent, Kc is also used to predict:
options: The direction of a chemical reaction
The colour of the products formed
The melting point of the reactants
The atomic masses of the elements
mcqs.why: Kc is used to predict the direction of a chemical reaction and, after a specific time, its extent; it also helps calculate the effect of changing conditions so the yield can be controlled.

mcqs.q: For the ammonia reaction, the Kp expression is:
mcqs.why: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g) at 450 C, Kp = (NH3)^2 / ((N2) (H2)^3) in partial pressures: products on top raised to their coefficients, reactants below raised to theirs.

mcqs.q: Controlling the yield of a reversible reaction with the help of Kc is useful because it:
options: Removes the need for raw materials
Decreases the expenditure of preparation, so product prices can be controlled to a desired level
mcqs.why: Kc helps calculate the effect of changing conditions, so the yield can be controlled; this decreases the expenditure of preparation and product prices can be controlled to a desired level.

mcqs.q: Ammonia obtained from the equilibrium reaction is mainly used to synthesize:
mcqs.why: For NH3, used in the synthesis of urea fertilizer, the reaction is N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g); more NH3 formed means more urea can be formed.

mcqs.q: The molecular formula of urea given in this lesson is:
mcqs.why: Kc is used industrially for compounds like sulphuric acid H2SO4, nitric acid HNO3 and urea, whose formula is written CO(NH2)2.

lessons.title: 10.1 Concepts of Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
General Properties of Acids

The word acid comes from Latin acidus meaning sour. Acids taste sour: acetic acid in vinegar, citric acid in lemons, grapefruit, oranges and limes, and lactic acid in sour milk, yogurt and cottage cheese, formed by fermentation of lactose sugar. Citrus sourness is also due to ascorbic acid.

  • Acids turn blue litmus red. Litmus is the oldest known pH indicator: red in acid, blue in base.
  • Acids corrode active metals: acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen gas. Even gold is attacked by aqua regia, a mixture of acids.
  • Acid solutions conduct electricity because acids ionize in water and ions are present.

General Properties of Bases

Bases taste bitter, turn red litmus blue and have a slippery, soapy touch in dilute solution. Strong concentrated acids and bases are corrosive and must not be touched.

Arrhenius Concept

According to Arrhenius, an acid yields hydrogen / hydronium ions in water, e.g. HCl(aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq), and a base yields hydroxide ions, e.g. NaOH(aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq). This concept is limited to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic character of ammonia, NH3.

Key Points

  • Acids are sour, turn blue litmus red, corrode metals giving H2, and conduct electricity in water.
  • Bases are bitter and slippery, and turn red litmus blue.
  • Arrhenius: acid gives H+ in water; base gives OH- in water.
  • Arrhenius concept works only for aqueous solutions.

mcqs.q: The word 'acid' comes from the Latin word 'acidus', which means:
mcqs.why: The word acid comes from Latin acidus meaning sour. Acids taste sour: acetic acid in vinegar, citric acid in citrus fruits and lactic acid in sour milk.

mcqs.q: The sour taste of lemons, oranges and grapefruit is due to:
options: Citric acid (and ascorbic acid in citrus fruits)
mcqs.why: Citric acid is present in lemons, grapefruit, oranges and limes, and citrus sourness is also due to ascorbic acid. Acetic acid is in vinegar and lactic acid in sour milk.

mcqs.q: Acids turn blue litmus paper:
mcqs.why: Acids turn blue litmus red. Litmus is the oldest known pH indicator: it is red in acid and blue in base, while bases turn red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with an active metal, the products are:
mcqs.why: Acids corrode active metals: acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen gas. This is one of the general properties of acids.

mcqs.q: Acid solutions conduct electricity because:
options: Acids ionize in water and ions are present in the solution
Acids contain free electrons like metals
mcqs.why: Acid solutions conduct electricity because acids ionize in water and ions are present; it is the movement of these ions that carries the current.

mcqs.q: Which is a general property of bases?
options: They taste sour and turn blue litmus red
They taste bitter, feel slippery and soapy in dilute solution, and turn red litmus blue
They corrode metals producing hydrogen gas
mcqs.why: Bases taste bitter, turn red litmus blue and have a slippery, soapy touch in dilute solution. Sour taste and turning blue litmus red are properties of acids.

mcqs.q: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid is a substance that:
options: Accepts a pair of electrons from another substance
Donates a proton to any substance in any solvent
Yields hydrogen (hydronium) ions in water, e.g. HCl(aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)
mcqs.why: According to Arrhenius, an acid yields hydrogen/hydronium ions in water, e.g. HCl(aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq), and a base yields hydroxide ions, e.g. NaOH(aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq).

mcqs.q: According to Arrhenius, NaOH is a base because in water it gives:
mcqs.why: A base, according to Arrhenius, yields hydroxide ions in water: NaOH(aq) -> Na+(aq) + OH-(aq). An acid yields H+ ions instead.

mcqs.q: A limitation of the Arrhenius concept is that it:
options: Is limited to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic character of ammonia, NH3
Cannot explain the behaviour of HCl in water
mcqs.why: The Arrhenius concept is limited to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic character of ammonia, NH3, which contains no OH- group yet behaves as a base.

mcqs.q: Even gold is attacked by aqua regia, which is:
mcqs.why: Acids corrode active metals, and even gold is attacked by aqua regia, a mixture of acids. This shows the corrosive power of acids.

lessons.title: 10.1.2 The Bronsted-Lowry Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Bronsted-Lowry Definitions (1923)

In 1923 J.N. Bronsted and T.M. Lowry independently proposed a broader concept. A Bronsted-Lowry acid is any substance capable of donating a proton (H+) to another substance. A Bronsted-Lowry base is any substance capable of accepting a proton (H+). A proton is what is left when a hydrogen atom loses an electron to become an ion.

HCl(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq): HCl is the acid, H2O is the base as it accepts H+. H2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + HSO4-(aq).

Conjugate Acids and Bases

When HCl transfers H+ to H2O, the H3O+ formed is the conjugate acid (formed from the parent base) and Cl- is the conjugate base (formed from the parent acid). Similarly HSO4- is a conjugate base.

Polyprotic Acids and Strength

Acids that can donate more than one proton are polyprotic acids, e.g. H2SO4 and H3PO4. Strength depends on tendency to donate / accept protons: HCl is a very strong acid, while citric acid in lemon is relatively weaker. This theory cannot explain the acidic character of SO2, NO2, AlCl3 and BF3, or the basic character of CaO and MgO.

Key Points

  • Bronsted-Lowry acid = proton (H+) donor; base = proton acceptor.
  • Conjugate acid forms from a base; conjugate base forms from an acid.
  • H2SO4 and H3PO4 are polyprotic acids.
  • Stronger acids donate protons more readily; stronger bases accept them more readily.

mcqs.q: The Bronsted-Lowry concept was proposed in 1923 by:
options: J. N. Bronsted and T. M. Lowry, independently
mcqs.why: In 1923 J. N. Bronsted and T. M. Lowry independently proposed a broader concept of acids and bases based on proton transfer.

mcqs.q: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a substance that:
options: Can accept a pair of electrons
Can donate a proton (H+) to another substance
Can accept a proton (H+) from another substance
mcqs.why: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is any substance capable of donating a proton (H+) to another substance, while a Bronsted-Lowry base is any substance capable of accepting a proton.

mcqs.q: In the reaction HCl(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq), water acts as:
options: An acid, because it donates an H+
A base, because it accepts an H+ from HCl
mcqs.why: HCl is the acid as it donates H+, and H2O is the base as it accepts H+ to form H3O+. The H3O+ formed is the conjugate acid and Cl- is the conjugate base.

mcqs.q: A proton is:
options: What is left when a hydrogen atom loses an electron to become an ion, i.e. H+
A hydrogen atom with an extra electron
The nucleus of a helium atom
mcqs.why: A proton is what is left when a hydrogen atom loses an electron to become an ion. Bronsted-Lowry acids donate this proton and bases accept it.

mcqs.q: When HCl transfers H+ to H2O, the Cl- left behind is called:
options: The conjugate base, formed from the parent acid
mcqs.why: When HCl transfers H+ to H2O, the H3O+ formed is the conjugate acid (formed from the parent base) and Cl- is the conjugate base (formed from the parent acid).

mcqs.q: Which of the following are polyprotic acids?
mcqs.why: Acids that can donate more than one proton are polyprotic acids, e.g. H2SO4 and H3PO4. H2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + HSO4-(aq) shows its first proton donation.

mcqs.q: In the reaction H2SO4(aq) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + HSO4-(aq), the HSO4- ion is:
mcqs.why: HSO4- is formed when the acid H2SO4 loses a proton, so it is a conjugate base, just as Cl- is the conjugate base of HCl.

mcqs.q: According to Bronsted-Lowry, the strength of an acid depends on:
options: Its tendency to donate protons; HCl is a very strong acid while citric acid is relatively weaker
The number of oxygen atoms it contains
mcqs.why: Strength depends on the tendency to donate or accept protons: HCl is a very strong acid, while citric acid in lemon is relatively weaker. Stronger bases accept protons more readily.

mcqs.q: A conjugate acid is formed from:
options: An acid, after it donates a proton
A base, after it accepts a proton
A salt, after it dissolves in water
A metal, after it reacts with an acid
mcqs.why: The conjugate acid forms from a base: when H2O accepts H+ it becomes H3O+, the conjugate acid. The conjugate base forms from an acid, e.g. Cl- from HCl.

mcqs.q: The Bronsted-Lowry theory cannot explain:
options: The reaction of HCl with water
The formation of conjugate acid-base pairs
The acidic character of SO2, NO2, AlCl3 and BF3, or the basic character of CaO and MgO
The strength of H2SO4 as an acid
mcqs.why: This theory cannot explain the acidic character of SO2, NO2, AlCl3 and BF3, or the basic character of CaO and MgO, because no proton transfer is involved in their behaviour.

lessons.title: 10.1.3 The Lewis Concept
lessons.notes_html:
Lewis Definitions (1923)

In 1923 G. N. Lewis (1875-1946) gave a more general concept, based on electron pairs instead of only proton transfer. When H+ combines with OH- to form water, H+ accepts a pair of electrons from OH- to form a new covalent bond.

  • Lewis acid: any substance that can act as an electron-pair acceptor, e.g. the H+ ion. Anything with one or more empty valence-shell orbitals can act as a Lewis acid.
  • Lewis base: any substance that can act as an electron-pair donor, e.g. the OH- ion. Every Bronsted base must have a pair of nonbonding electrons to accept a proton.

Example: BF3 and NH3

BF3 reacts instantaneously with NH3. The nonbonding electrons on nitrogen in NH3 are donated into an empty orbital on boron in BF3, forming a new type of covalent bond called a coordinate covalent bond: BF3 + NH3 -> BF3-NH3.

The Lewis concept has a marked edge over previous theories: it explains not only hydrogen-containing acids but also species that lack H+, and explains bases in a comprehensive manner.

Key Points

  • Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
  • H+ is a Lewis acid and OH- is a Lewis base.
  • NH3 donates its lone pair to BF3, forming a coordinate covalent bond.
  • Lewis theory is the broadest of the three concepts.

mcqs.q: The Lewis concept of acids and bases was given in 1923 by:
mcqs.why: In 1923 G. N. Lewis (1875-1946) gave a more general concept of acids and bases, based on electron pairs instead of only proton transfer.

mcqs.q: A Lewis acid is a substance that:
options: Can act as an electron-pair donor
Donates a proton to a base
Can act as an electron-pair acceptor
mcqs.why: A Lewis acid is any substance that can act as an electron-pair acceptor, e.g. the H+ ion; anything with one or more empty valence-shell orbitals can act as a Lewis acid.

mcqs.q: A Lewis base is a substance that:
options: Can act as an electron-pair donor, e.g. the OH- ion
Can act as an electron-pair acceptor
mcqs.why: A Lewis base is any substance that can act as an electron-pair donor, e.g. the OH- ion. Every Bronsted base must have a pair of nonbonding electrons to accept a proton.

mcqs.q: When H+ combines with OH- to form water, the H+ acts as a Lewis acid because it:
options: Donates a pair of electrons to OH-
Accepts a pair of electrons from OH- to form a new covalent bond
mcqs.why: When H+ combines with OH- to form water, H+ accepts a pair of electrons from OH- to form a new covalent bond, which is exactly the Lewis definition of an acid.

mcqs.q: In the reaction BF3 + NH3 -> BF3-NH3, the new bond formed is called a:
mcqs.why: The nonbonding electrons on nitrogen in NH3 are donated into an empty orbital on boron in BF3, forming a new type of covalent bond called a coordinate covalent bond.

mcqs.q: In the BF3 and NH3 reaction, NH3 acts as a Lewis base because:
options: It donates a proton to BF3
It accepts an electron pair from BF3
It produces OH- ions in water
Its nitrogen donates its nonbonding electron pair into the empty orbital of boron in BF3
mcqs.why: BF3 reacts instantaneously with NH3: the lone pair on nitrogen is donated into an empty orbital on boron, so NH3 is the electron-pair donor (Lewis base) and BF3 the acceptor (Lewis acid).

mcqs.q: Anything with one or more empty valence-shell orbitals can act as a:
mcqs.why: Anything with one or more empty valence-shell orbitals can act as a Lewis acid, because it can accept an electron pair into the empty orbital, as boron in BF3 does.

mcqs.q: The Lewis concept is broader than the earlier concepts because it:
options: Explains not only hydrogen-containing acids but also species that lack H+, and explains bases comprehensively
Is based only on the taste of substances
mcqs.why: The Lewis concept has a marked edge over previous theories: it explains species that lack H+, such as BF3 and AlCl3, as well as hydrogen-containing acids, and explains bases in a comprehensive manner.

mcqs.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: H+ is a Lewis base and OH- is a Lewis acid
Both H+ and OH- are Lewis acids
H+ is a Lewis acid and OH- is a Lewis base
Both H+ and OH- are Lewis bases
mcqs.why: H+ accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid; OH- donates an electron pair, so it is a Lewis base. Together they form water by a new covalent bond.

mcqs.q: Every Bronsted base must have:
options: A hydroxide group in its formula
A metal atom in its structure
A pair of nonbonding electrons, with which it accepts a proton
mcqs.why: Every Bronsted base must have a pair of nonbonding electrons to accept a proton. This links the Bronsted and Lewis ideas: the same lone pair that accepts H+ makes it a Lewis base too.

lessons.title: 10.2 The pH Scale (Hydrogen Ion Concentration)
lessons.notes_html:
Self-Ionization of Water and pH

Water molecules react with each other: H2O(l) + H2O(l) -> H3O+(aq) + OH-(aq). This is the self-ionization of water. Its dissociation constant is Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14. In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7.

pH = -log[H+]. For pure water, -log[H+] = 7, so pH 7 is neutral. pH 1 to 6.9 is acidic, pH 7.1 to 14.0 is basic. Lower pH means more acidic: pH 2 is more acidic than pH 3. Higher pH means more basic: pH 10 is more basic than pH 8.

Example 10.1: If [H+] = 0.0001 moles/lit = 1 x 10^-4, then pH = -log(1 x 10^-4) = 4.

pH of Common Substances (Table 10.1)

pHSubstancepHSubstance
1Hydrochloric acid / battery acid7Pure water
2Gastric fluid7.4Blood
3Lemon juice, vinegar8Egg white, baking soda
5Black coffee10Soapy solutions, milk of magnesia
6.7Milk14Caustic soda

10.2.1 Indicators

IndicatorIn acidIn base
PhenolphthaleinColourlessPink / purple
LitmusRedBlue
Methyl orangeRedYellow

Universal indicator, made by mixing various indicators, shows different colours at different pH. Natural pigments called anthocyanins in beetroot and red cabbage also act as indicators, ranging red to purple to blue.

Key Points

  • Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14; pure water has pH 7.
  • pH = -log[H+]; pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic.
  • As pH decreases, [H+] and acidic character increase.
  • Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.

mcqs.q: The dissociation constant of water, Kw, is equal to:
mcqs.why: Water self-ionizes: H2O + H2O -> H3O+ + OH-. Its dissociation constant is Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14, and in pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7.

mcqs.q: The pH of a solution is defined as:
mcqs.why: pH = -log[H+]. For pure water, -log(1 x 10^-7) = 7, so pH 7 is neutral; pH 1 to 6.9 is acidic and pH 7.1 to 14.0 is basic.

mcqs.q: If [H+] = 0.0001 mol/litre = 1 x 10^-4, the pH of the solution is:
mcqs.why: Working (Example 10.1 of the book): pH = -log[H+] = -log(1 x 10^-4) = 4. The exponent of 10, with sign changed, directly gives the pH for such concentrations.

mcqs.q: A solution has [H+] = 1 x 10^-2 mol/litre. Its pH is:
mcqs.why: Working: pH = -log[H+] = -log(1 x 10^-2) = 2. A pH of 2 lies in the acidic range 1 to 6.9, like gastric fluid which also has pH 2.

mcqs.q: For a solution with [H+] = 1 x 10^-3 mol/litre, the hydroxide ion concentration [OH-] is:
mcqs.why: Working: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1 x 10^-14, so [OH-] = Kw / [H+] = (1 x 10^-14) / (1 x 10^-3) = 1 x 10^-11 mol/litre. The exponents subtract: -14 - (-3) = -11.

mcqs.q: Which statement about pH is correct?
options: Lower pH means more acidic: pH 2 is more acidic than pH 3, and pH 10 is more basic than pH 8
Higher pH means more acidic: pH 3 is more acidic than pH 2
pH 7 is the most acidic value on the scale
pH values below 7 are basic and above 7 are acidic
mcqs.why: Lower pH means more acidic: pH 2 is more acidic than pH 3. Higher pH means more basic: pH 10 is more basic than pH 8. As pH decreases, [H+] and acidic character increase.

mcqs.q: According to Table 10.1, the pH of blood is:
mcqs.why: Table 10.1 lists blood at pH 7.4, slightly basic. Pure water is 7, milk is 6.7, gastric fluid is 2 and black coffee is 5.

mcqs.q: Phenolphthalein indicator is:
options: Pink in acid and colourless in base
Red in acid and yellow in base
Colourless in acid and pink/purple in base
Blue in acid and red in base
mcqs.why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink/purple in base. Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base, and litmus is red in acid and blue in base.

mcqs.q: Methyl orange indicator shows which colours?
options: Colourless in acid and pink in base
Blue in acid and red in base
Yellow in acid and red in base
Red in acid and yellow in base
mcqs.why: From the indicator table: methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base, whereas phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base.

mcqs.q: Natural pigments that act as indicators, found in beetroot and red cabbage, are called:
mcqs.why: Natural pigments called anthocyanins in beetroot and red cabbage act as indicators, ranging red to purple to blue. Universal indicator, a mixture of various indicators, shows different colours at different pH.

lessons.title: 10.3 The Salts
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Salt?

Salts are the neutralization products when an acid reacts with a base: HCl(aq) + NaOH(s) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Similarly H2SO4(aq) + 2KOH(aq) -> K2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l). Salts are ionic compounds with high melting and boiling points, e.g. NaCl melts at 801 C. Thousands of salts exist and most inorganic compounds belong to this class.

Some Common Salts (Table 10.2)

NameFormulaUsage
Sodium chlorideNaClUsed in food
Potassium sulphateK2SO4Found in salinity affected areas; used in making explosives
Ammonium chlorideNH4ClUsed in cough medicines
Ammonium phosphate(NH4)3PO4Used as fertilizer
Silver nitrateAgNO3Used in photography
Copper sulphateCuSO4Poisonous; used in medicines in very little quantity
Washing sodaNa2CO3.10H2OUsed in laundry
Baking sodaNaHCO3Used in bakery, cooking

Colour, Taste and Odour

Many salts are coloured: yellow sodium chromate, orange potassium dichromate, blue copper sulfate pentahydrate, colourless magnesium sulfate. Salts show all five tastes: salty NaCl, sour potassium bitartrate, bitter magnesium sulfate, and umami monosodium glutamate. Salts of strong acids and strong bases are non-volatile and odourless.

Key Points

  • A salt plus water is formed when an acid neutralizes a base.
  • Salts are ionic, with high melting and boiling points; NaCl melts at 801 C.
  • NaCl is used in food, (NH4)3PO4 as fertilizer and AgNO3 in photography.
  • Potassium dichromate is orange and copper sulphate is blue.

mcqs.q: A salt is formed when:
options: An acid reacts with a base in a neutralization reaction, giving a salt and water
A metal reacts with oxygen in air
An acid is diluted with water
mcqs.why: Salts are the neutralization products when an acid reacts with a base: HCl(aq) + NaOH(s) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Similarly H2SO4 + 2KOH -> K2SO4 + 2H2O.

mcqs.q: Salts are ionic compounds, and as a result they have:
options: Low melting and boiling points like organic compounds
High melting and boiling points; NaCl, for example, melts at 801 C
No definite melting point at all
mcqs.why: Salts are ionic compounds with high melting and boiling points, e.g. NaCl melts at 801 C. Thousands of salts exist and most inorganic compounds belong to this class.

mcqs.q: Which salt is used as a fertilizer?
mcqs.why: From Table 10.2: ammonium phosphate (NH4)3PO4 is used as fertilizer, AgNO3 is used in photography, NH4Cl in cough medicines and NaCl in food.

mcqs.q: Silver nitrate, AgNO3, is used in:
mcqs.why: Table 10.2 lists silver nitrate AgNO3 as used in photography. Washing soda is used in laundry and baking soda in bakery and cooking.

mcqs.q: The formulae of washing soda and baking soda are:
options: Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O and baking soda NaHCO3
Washing soda NaHCO3 and baking soda Na2CO3.10H2O
Washing soda NaCl and baking soda NaOH
mcqs.why: Washing soda is Na2CO3.10H2O, used in laundry, while baking soda is NaHCO3, used in bakery and cooking, as given in the table of common salts.

mcqs.q: Ammonium chloride, NH4Cl, is used in:
mcqs.why: Table 10.2 shows ammonium chloride NH4Cl is used in cough medicines. Potassium sulphate K2SO4 is found in salinity affected areas and used in making explosives.

mcqs.q: Which salt is orange in colour?
mcqs.why: Many salts are coloured: yellow sodium chromate, orange potassium dichromate, blue copper sulfate pentahydrate and colourless magnesium sulfate.

mcqs.q: The umami taste among salts is shown by:
mcqs.why: Salts show all five tastes: salty NaCl, sour potassium bitartrate, bitter magnesium sulfate, and umami monosodium glutamate. Salts of strong acids and strong bases are non-volatile and odourless.

mcqs.q: Copper sulphate, CuSO4, is used in medicines only in very small quantity because it is:
mcqs.why: Table 10.2 notes that copper sulphate CuSO4 is poisonous and is used in medicines in very little quantity. It is the blue salt among the common salts listed.

mcqs.q: The neutralization reaction between sulphuric acid and potassium hydroxide gives:
mcqs.why: Salts are neutralization products: H2SO4(aq) + 2KOH(aq) -> K2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l). Two KOH are needed to neutralize both replaceable hydrogens of H2SO4, and water is always the other product.

lessons.title: 10.3.1 Preparation of Salts
lessons.notes_html:
Natural Sources

Many salts are obtained by mining: CaCO3 (lime and marble), halite NaCl, gypsum CaSO4.2H2O and NaHCO3. In Pakistan the world's second largest halite mine is at Khewra, near Jhelum. NaCl is also got by evaporating sea water.

Preparation of Soluble Salts

  • Acid + base: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
  • Acid + metal: H2SO4 + 2Na -> Na2SO4 + H2; 2HCl + Ca -> CaCl2 + H2.
  • Acid + metallic oxide: 2HCl + CuO -> CuCl2 + H2O; H2SO4 + MgO -> MgSO4 + H2O.
  • Acid + metal carbonate: H2SO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2.

Insoluble salts are made by precipitation: mix two soluble salt solutions and filter off the precipitate, e.g. CaCl2 + K2SO4 -> 2KCl + CaSO4(s).

10.3.2 Types of Salts

  • Normal / neutral: no H+ or OH- in water, e.g. NaCl, KCl, K2SO4.
  • Acidic: produce H+ or accept a lone pair, e.g. KHSO4, AlCl3, NH4Cl.
  • Basic: produce OH- or accept H+, e.g. Na2CO3.10H2O, NaHCO3, CH3COONa.
  • Double: made of two salts, e.g. Mohr's salt FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O and potash alum.

10.3.3 Uses of Salts

Uses: in food (NaCl, monosodium glutamate, NaHCO3), as pigments (orange K2Cr2O7, green NiCl2, yellow CdS), as preservatives (Na2S2O5, NaCl), in medicines (Epsom salt MgSO4.7H2O as purgative, fluoride salts for tooth decay, calcium salts for bones), as fertilizers (KNO3, ammonium phosphate), in glass making (sodium silicate) and as bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl. Sea water has about 35,000 ppm salt; it is desalinated by reverse osmosis.

Key Points

  • Soluble salts are made by acid with base, metal, metal oxide or metal carbonate.
  • Insoluble salts are made by precipitation and separated by filtration.
  • Salts are normal, acidic, basic or double salts.
  • Khewra has the world's second largest halite mine.

mcqs.q: The world's second largest halite (rock salt) mine is located at:
mcqs.why: Many salts are obtained by mining. In Pakistan the world's second largest halite mine is at Khewra, near Jhelum; NaCl is also obtained by evaporating sea water.

mcqs.q: The formula of gypsum, a naturally occurring salt, is:
mcqs.why: Salts obtained from natural sources include CaCO3 (lime and marble), halite NaCl, gypsum CaSO4.2H2O and NaHCO3, all obtained by mining or evaporation.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid reacting with sodium metal gives:
mcqs.why: Soluble salts are prepared by acid + metal: H2SO4 + 2Na -> Na2SO4 + H2. Similarly 2HCl + Ca -> CaCl2 + H2; hydrogen gas is always evolved with metals.

mcqs.q: Copper(II) oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid gives:
mcqs.why: Acid + metallic oxide gives a soluble salt and water: 2HCl + CuO -> CuCl2 + H2O. Similarly H2SO4 + MgO -> MgSO4 + H2O.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, the products are:
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide, e.g. H2SO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2
Only a salt and carbon dioxide, with no water
mcqs.why: Acid + metal carbonate is a standard preparation of soluble salts: H2SO4 + Na2CO3 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2. The CO2 gas is the extra product compared with acid + base.

mcqs.q: Insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation, for example:
options: Heating CaCO3 strongly in a furnace
Evaporating sea water in shallow pits
CaCl2 + K2SO4 -> 2KCl + CaSO4(s), and the precipitate is filtered off
Reacting Ca metal with dilute H2SO4
mcqs.why: Insoluble salts are made by precipitation: mix two soluble salt solutions and filter off the precipitate, e.g. CaCl2 + K2SO4 -> 2KCl + CaSO4(s), where (s) shows the insoluble solid.

mcqs.q: Normal (neutral) salts are those which:
options: Are made of two different salts combined
Produce neither H+ nor OH- in water, e.g. NaCl, KCl and K2SO4
mcqs.why: Normal/neutral salts have no H+ or OH- in water, e.g. NaCl, KCl, K2SO4. Acidic salts produce H+, basic salts produce OH-, and double salts are made of two salts.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an acidic salt?
mcqs.why: Acidic salts produce H+ or accept a lone pair, e.g. KHSO4, AlCl3, NH4Cl. NaHCO3 and CH3COONa are basic salts, and NaCl is a normal salt.

mcqs.q: Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, is an example of a:
mcqs.why: Double salts are made of two salts, e.g. Mohr's salt FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O and potash alum. This completes the four types: normal, acidic, basic and double salts.

mcqs.q: Sea water contains about 35,000 ppm of salt, and it is desalinated by:
mcqs.why: The uses section notes that sea water has about 35,000 ppm salt and it is desalinated by reverse osmosis. Salts are also used in food, pigments, preservatives, medicines, fertilizers and glass making.

lessons.title: 11.1 Introduction to Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
What is Organic Chemistry?

Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. Carbon is the chief element in organic compounds. Examples are methane CH4, glucose C6H12O6, urea and proteins.

Compounds containing carbon but studied as inorganic include oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates, cyanides and carbides, e.g. NaHCO3 is inorganic.

Vital Force Theory and Wohler

Berzelius in 1815 proposed the vital force theory: organic compounds could only be made by living organisms with a vital force. In 1828 Wohler broke this theory by preparing urea, the first synthetic organic compound, in the laboratory by heating ammonium cyanate: NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2 (urea). After this, many organic compounds were synthesised in laboratories.

Key Points

  • Organic chemistry studies hydrocarbons and their derivatives; carbon is the chief element.
  • Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen, e.g. CH4.
  • Vital force theory (Berzelius, 1815) said organic compounds need a living source.
  • Wohler (1828) made urea from ammonium cyanate, ending vitalism.

mcqs.q: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with:
mcqs.why: Organic chemistry deals with hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen, and carbon is the chief element in organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain:
options: Only carbon and hydrogen, e.g. methane CH4
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. Examples of organic compounds are methane CH4, glucose C6H12O6, urea and proteins.

mcqs.q: Although NaHCO3 contains carbon, it is studied as an inorganic compound because it is a:
options: Bicarbonate; carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides of carbon, cyanides and carbides are treated as inorganic
mcqs.why: Compounds containing carbon but studied as inorganic include oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates, cyanides and carbides, e.g. NaHCO3 is inorganic.

mcqs.q: The vital force theory, proposed by Berzelius in 1815, stated that:
options: Organic compounds can be made easily in any laboratory
Carbon can form long chains with itself
Organic compounds could only be made by living organisms with a vital force
mcqs.why: Berzelius in 1815 proposed the vital force theory: organic compounds could only be made by living organisms with a vital force. The theory stood until Wohler's experiment in 1828.

mcqs.q: Wohler broke the vital force theory in 1828 by:
options: Preparing urea, the first synthetic organic compound, in the laboratory by heating ammonium cyanate
mcqs.why: In 1828 Wohler prepared urea by heating ammonium cyanate: NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2 (urea). After this, many organic compounds were synthesised in laboratories.

mcqs.q: The reaction NH4CNO -> NH2CONH2 shows the preparation of:
mcqs.why: Wohler heated ammonium cyanate NH4CNO and obtained NH2CONH2, urea, the first synthetic organic compound, without any living organism or vital force.

mcqs.q: The chief element in all organic compounds is:
mcqs.why: Carbon is the chief element in organic compounds such as methane CH4, glucose C6H12O6, urea and proteins. Hydrocarbons additionally contain only hydrogen with carbon.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an organic compound?
mcqs.why: Glucose C6H12O6 is listed among the examples of organic compounds, while carbonates, bicarbonates and oxides of carbon such as CaCO3, NaHCO3 and CO2 are studied as inorganic.

mcqs.q: After Wohler's synthesis of urea, what happened in chemistry?
options: Many organic compounds began to be synthesised in laboratories
The vital force theory became stronger
Organic chemistry was abandoned as a subject
mcqs.why: After Wohler made urea in the laboratory in 1828, the vital force theory ended and many organic compounds were synthesised in laboratories from inorganic starting materials.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only compounds studied as inorganic despite containing carbon?
options: Oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates, cyanides and carbides
mcqs.why: The lesson lists oxides of carbon, carbonates, bicarbonates, cyanides and carbides as carbon compounds studied in inorganic chemistry; hydrocarbons and their derivatives belong to organic chemistry.

lessons.title: 11.1 Features of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
General Characteristics

  • Mostly covalent compounds, generally non-polar.
  • Insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents.
  • Low melting and boiling points; mostly liquids or low-melting solids, volatile and inflammable.
  • Reactions are slow and often need heat, pressure or a catalyst.
  • Show isomerism: same molecular formula, different structures, e.g. butane and isobutane, both C4H10.

Catenation and Homologous Series

Catenation is the ability of carbon to link with itself to form long straight chains, branched chains and rings. This is why millions of organic compounds exist.

A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, where each member differs by a -CH2- unit and physical properties change regularly. In alkanes boiling point rises with chain length: methane (1 C) -162 C, ethane (2 C) -89 C, propane (3 C) -42 C, butane (4 C) 0 C, pentane (5 C) 36 C, n-hexane (6 C) 69 C.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds are covalent, non-polar, water-insoluble and have low melting/boiling points.
  • Catenation = carbon forming long chains, branches and rings with itself.
  • Homologous series members differ by CH2, share chemical properties.
  • Isomers have the same formula but different structures.

mcqs.q: Most organic compounds are:
mcqs.why: Organic compounds are mostly covalent compounds and generally non-polar. This is why they are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds are generally:
options: Soluble in water but insoluble in organic solvents
Soluble in both water and acids only
Insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents
mcqs.why: Being covalent and non-polar, organic compounds are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents, and they have low melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: Which property is typical of organic compounds?
options: Very high melting points like salts
They are all gases at room temperature
Low melting and boiling points; mostly liquids or low-melting solids, volatile and inflammable
mcqs.why: Organic compounds have low melting and boiling points; they are mostly liquids or low-melting solids, volatile and inflammable, and their reactions are slow, often needing heat, pressure or a catalyst.

mcqs.q: Isomerism is shown by butane and isobutane because they:
options: Have the same molecular formula C4H10 but different structures
Have the same structure but different names only
mcqs.why: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures, e.g. butane and isobutane, both C4H10. Isomerism is one of the characteristic features of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Catenation is the ability of carbon to:
options: Form four bonds with hydrogen only
Link with itself to form long straight chains, branched chains and rings
mcqs.why: Catenation is the ability of carbon to link with itself to form long straight chains, branched chains and rings. This is why millions of organic compounds exist.

mcqs.q: In a homologous series, each member differs from the next by:
options: One carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms
A -CH2- unit, while the functional group and chemical properties remain similar
A complete change of functional group
mcqs.why: A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, where each member differs by a -CH2- unit and physical properties change regularly.

mcqs.q: The boiling points of methane (-162 C) and n-hexane (69 C) differ by:
mcqs.why: Working: difference = 69 - (-162) = 69 + 162 = 231 C. In the alkane series the boiling point rises regularly with chain length: methane -162, ethane -89, propane -42, butane 0, pentane 36 and n-hexane 69 C.

mcqs.q: In the homologous series of alkanes, as the chain length increases, the boiling point:
options: Rises regularly, e.g. methane -162 C up to n-hexane 69 C
First falls and then becomes zero
mcqs.why: Physical properties change regularly in a homologous series: methane (1 C) boils at -162 C, ethane -89 C, propane -42 C, butane 0 C, pentane 36 C and n-hexane (6 C) at 69 C.

mcqs.q: Reactions of organic compounds are usually:
options: Slow and often need heat, pressure or a catalyst
mcqs.why: Unlike many inorganic reactions, organic reactions are slow and often need heat, pressure or a catalyst to proceed at a useful rate.

mcqs.q: Members of the same homologous series have similar chemical properties because they have:
options: The same number of carbon atoms
mcqs.why: A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and similar chemical properties; members differ by -CH2- and show a regular change in physical properties.

lessons.title: 11.2 Sources of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Main Sources

The main source is the plant kingdom (photosynthesis in green plants). Animals get organic compounds from plants. Buried decayed plants and animals, under heat and pressure, formed coal, petroleum and natural gas.

11.2.1 Coal

TypeCarbon %Use
Anthracitemore than 90%Top quality fuel
Bituminous80%Domestic fuel in cold regions of Pakistan
Lignite70%Power stations for electricity
Peatabout 60%Low-cost furnace fuel, e.g. brick kilns; inferior due to high moisture

11.2.2 Petroleum and 11.2.3 Natural Gas

Petroleum (Petra = rock, Oleum = oil) is a blackish viscous liquid, a mixture of hundreds of compounds. It is purified by fractional distillation on the basis of different boiling points: Refinery gases C1-C4 (cylinder gas), Gasoline C4-C8 (car fuel), Naphtha C5-C10 (making chemicals), Kerosene C12-C16 (aircraft fuel), Diesel C15-C18, Fuel oil C19-C30 (ships, power stations), Residue 400-600 C (bitumen for roads and roofs).

Natural gas, found at Sui, Balochistan in 1952, hence called Sui gas, contains: methane 70-90%, ethane 5-15%, propane less than 5%, butane 1-2%, rest N2, CO2, H2S. Used as fuel, CNG and for urea. In LPG, propane and butane proportion is higher to ease liquefaction.

11.2.4 Synthesis: many compounds are now made in laboratories/factories, e.g. plastics, urea, medicines, detergents, dyes, artificial fibres.

Key Points

  • Plants are the main source; coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from buried remains.
  • Anthracite >90% C is best coal; peat about 60% C is inferior.
  • Petroleum fractions are separated by fractional distillation by boiling point.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane 70-90%; Sui gas found in 1952.

mcqs.q: The main source of organic compounds is:
options: The plant kingdom, through photosynthesis in green plants
mcqs.why: The main source is the plant kingdom (photosynthesis in green plants). Animals get organic compounds from plants, and buried decayed plants and animals formed coal, petroleum and natural gas.

mcqs.q: Anthracite is the top quality coal because it contains:
mcqs.why: Anthracite contains more than 90% carbon and is the top quality fuel. Bituminous has 80%, lignite 70% and peat about 60% carbon.

mcqs.q: Peat is an inferior fuel because:
options: It contains only about 60% carbon and has high moisture content
It is found only in very small amounts
mcqs.why: Peat has about 60% carbon and is a low-cost furnace fuel, e.g. for brick kilns, but it is inferior due to high moisture. Lignite (70% C) is used in power stations.

mcqs.q: Bituminous coal, with 80% carbon, is used as:
options: Domestic fuel in the cold regions of Pakistan
mcqs.why: The coal table shows bituminous (80% C) as domestic fuel in cold regions of Pakistan; lignite (70%) is used in power stations for electricity and peat in brick kiln furnaces.

mcqs.q: Petroleum is purified by fractional distillation, separating fractions on the basis of:
mcqs.why: Petroleum is a mixture of hundreds of compounds purified by fractional distillation on the basis of different boiling points: refinery gases, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil and residue.

mcqs.q: Kerosene, the fraction with C12-C16, is used as:
mcqs.why: In the petroleum fractions: refinery gases C1-C4 are cylinder gas, gasoline C4-C8 is car fuel, naphtha C5-C10 is for making chemicals, kerosene C12-C16 is aircraft fuel and diesel C15-C18.

mcqs.q: Natural gas found at Sui, Balochistan in 1952 is mainly composed of:
mcqs.why: Sui gas contains methane 70-90%, ethane 5-15%, propane less than 5%, butane 1-2% and the rest N2, CO2 and H2S. It is used as fuel, CNG and for making urea.

mcqs.q: In LPG, compared with natural gas, the proportion of propane and butane is:
mcqs.why: In LPG, propane and butane proportion is higher to ease liquefaction, whereas natural gas is mostly methane. Natural gas is used as fuel, CNG and for urea manufacture.

mcqs.q: The residue fraction of petroleum, obtained at 400-600 C, is bitumen, used for:
mcqs.why: The residue (400-600 C) is bitumen for roads and roofs. Fuel oil C19-C30 is used for ships and power stations, and diesel C15-C18 for vehicles.

mcqs.q: Coal, petroleum and natural gas were formed from:
options: Buried decayed plants and animals under heat and pressure over a long time
mcqs.why: Buried decayed plants and animals, under heat and pressure, formed coal, petroleum and natural gas. Plants remain the main living source through photosynthesis.

lessons.title: 11.3 Uses of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Organic Compounds in Daily Life

Because of catenation, organic compounds are countless and are used at almost every step of daily life:

  • Food: vegetables, fruits, meat and cereals are organic compounds.
  • Clothing: natural fibres cotton and wool, and artificial fibres like rayon and plastic threads.
  • Medicines: antipyretics, anti-inflammatory drugs, antihistamines, antibiotics and anti-ulcer drugs.
  • Fertilisers: urea and others increase crop production.
  • Insecticides and fungicides: used against insect and fungus attack.
  • Fuels: natural gas, petrol, kerosene oil, diesel, CNG, LPG, coal and wood.
  • Dyes: give colour in daily life.
  • Plastics: used in various fields of life.

Key Points

  • Food, clothes, medicines, fertilisers and fuels are mostly organic compounds.
  • Medicines such as antibiotics and antipyretics are organic.
  • Urea fertiliser, dyes, plastics and fibres are important uses.
  • Organic chemistry affects almost every part of our life.

mcqs.q: Which of the following medicines are organic compounds?
options: Only mineral salts and metal oxides
Only vitamins made in the body
Antipyretics, anti-inflammatory drugs, antihistamines, antibiotics and anti-ulcer drugs
mcqs.why: Medicines such as antipyretics, anti-inflammatory drugs, antihistamines, antibiotics and anti-ulcer drugs are organic compounds, one of the major uses of organic compounds in daily life.

mcqs.q: Natural fibres cotton and wool, and artificial fibres like rayon, are examples of organic compounds used in:
mcqs.why: In clothing we use natural fibres cotton and wool and artificial fibres like rayon and plastic threads, all organic compounds. Food, medicines, fertilisers and fuels are other everyday uses.

mcqs.q: Urea is an important organic compound used as a:
mcqs.why: Fertilisers such as urea increase crop production. Urea was also the first organic compound synthesised in a laboratory, by Wohler in 1828.

mcqs.q: Insecticides and fungicides are organic compounds used to:
options: Increase the octane number of petrol
Protect crops against insect and fungus attack
mcqs.why: Insecticides and fungicides are used against insect and fungus attack on crops. Fuels, dyes, plastics and fibres are other important uses of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only fuels that are organic compounds?
options: Common salt, washing soda and gypsum
Natural gas, petrol, kerosene oil, diesel, CNG, LPG, coal and wood
mcqs.why: Fuels such as natural gas, petrol, kerosene oil, diesel, CNG, LPG, coal and wood are organic compounds (or carbon-based fuels) used in daily life.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds are used at almost every step of daily life mainly because:
options: Catenation makes them countless in number
They are all soluble in water
They all have very high melting points
They are all made by living organisms only
mcqs.why: Because of catenation, organic compounds are countless and are used at almost every step of daily life: food, clothing, medicines, fertilisers, insecticides, fuels, dyes and plastics.

mcqs.q: Dyes, which give colour in daily life, belong to which class of compounds?
mcqs.why: Dyes are listed among the everyday uses of organic compounds, together with plastics, fibres, medicines and fertilisers.

mcqs.q: Plastics used in various fields of life are:
options: Natural minerals mined from the earth
mcqs.why: Many compounds are now made in laboratories and factories, e.g. plastics, urea, medicines, detergents, dyes and artificial fibres; plastics are used in various fields of life.

mcqs.q: The food we eat — vegetables, fruits, meat and cereals — consists largely of:
mcqs.why: Food items such as vegetables, fruits, meat and cereals are organic compounds, which is why organic chemistry affects almost every part of our life.

mcqs.q: Antibiotics and antipyretics are organic compounds used as:
mcqs.why: Medicines such as antibiotics and antipyretics are organic compounds. Antipyretics reduce fever and antibiotics fight bacterial infections.

lessons.title: 11.4 Alkanes and Alkyl Radicals
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes

Alkanes are the simplest class, with carbon linked by single covalent bonds only. General formula CnH2n+2. They are saturated hydrocarbons because each carbon forms its maximum 4 bonds. First members: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12, hexane C6H14, heptane C7H16, octane C8H18, nonane C9H20, decane C10H22. Condensed formula of hexane is CH3(CH2)4CH3. Compounds with same formula but different structures are isomers, e.g. butane/isobutane and pentane/isopentane/neopentane.

Alkanes are water-insoluble, less reactive, and burn to give much energy, so used as fuels: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + 891 KJ/mol; C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O + 2220 KJ/mol. Alkanes with more than 20 carbons are lubricants; paraffin wax (20-40 carbons) is used in candles, lubricants, water repellents and skin creams.

11.4.1 Alkyl Radicals and Classification

Removing one H from an alkane gives an alkyl group, written R-H for the class, with an unpaired electron: methane -> methyl .CH3, ethane -> ethyl .C2H5; also n-propyl, isopropyl, n-butyl, isobutyl. Suffix -ane changes to -yl.

Alkanes are classified as straight chain (each C bonded to max 2 other C, e.g. n-pentane), branched (at least one C bonded to 3 other C) and cyclic (closed ring, at least 3 C, e.g. cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclohexane). Carbon atoms may be primary (linked to 1 C), secondary (2 C), tertiary (3 C) or quaternary (4 C).

Key Points

  • Alkanes: CnH2n+2, single bonds, saturated hydrocarbons.
  • Combustion gives CO2 + H2O + heat; higher alkanes give more energy.
  • Alkyl radical = alkane minus one H, e.g. methyl .CH3.
  • Alkanes are straight chain, branched or cyclic.

mcqs.q: The general formula of alkanes is:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are the simplest class, with carbon linked by single covalent bonds only, and their general formula is CnH2n+2. Alkenes are CnH2n and alkynes CnH2n-2.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are called saturated hydrocarbons because:
options: Each carbon forms its maximum 4 bonds, with single covalent bonds only
mcqs.why: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons because each carbon forms its maximum 4 bonds and all carbon-carbon bonds are single covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n+2, the molecular formula of the alkane with 7 carbon atoms (heptane) is:
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 7, H = 2n + 2 = 2(7) + 2 = 16, so heptane is C7H16. The series runs CH4, C2H6, C3H8, C4H10, C5H12, C6H14, C7H16 and so on.

mcqs.q: The condensed formula of hexane is:
mcqs.why: The condensed formula of hexane is CH3(CH2)4CH3: two end CH3 groups with four CH2 groups between them give 6 carbons and 14 hydrogens, C6H14.

mcqs.q: Complete combustion of methane is shown by:
mcqs.why: Alkanes burn to give much energy: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + 891 KJ/mol. Propane gives even more: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O + 2220 KJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane gives:
options: An alkyl group (radical), e.g. methane gives methyl .CH3
mcqs.why: Removing one H from an alkane gives an alkyl group with an unpaired electron: methane -> methyl .CH3, ethane -> ethyl .C2H5. The suffix -ane changes to -yl.

mcqs.q: The ethyl radical obtained from ethane is:
mcqs.why: Ethane minus one H gives ethyl .C2H5, while methane minus one H gives methyl .CH3. Other alkyl groups include n-propyl, isopropyl, n-butyl and isobutyl.

mcqs.q: In a branched alkane, at least one carbon atom is bonded to:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are classified as straight chain (each C bonded to a maximum of 2 other C), branched (at least one C bonded to 3 other C) and cyclic (a closed ring of at least 3 C, e.g. cyclopropane).

mcqs.q: A tertiary carbon atom is one that is linked to:
mcqs.why: Carbon atoms may be primary (linked to 1 C), secondary (2 C), tertiary (3 C) or quaternary (4 C). This classification is used in describing alkane structures.

mcqs.q: Paraffin wax, containing 20-40 carbon atoms, is used in:
options: Candles, lubricants, water repellents and skin creams
mcqs.why: Alkanes with more than 20 carbons are lubricants; paraffin wax (20-40 carbons) is used in candles, lubricants, water repellents and skin creams. Alkanes are water-insoluble and less reactive.

lessons.title: 11.5 The Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Functional Group?

A functional group is the group of atom(s) upon which the functions or properties of an organic compound depend. It is the most reactive part of the compound. Compounds with the same functional group form the same homologous series, with same chemical properties. Fruit fragrance is due to the ester group, e.g. banana has isopentyl acetate, apple methyl butyrate, orange octyl acetate.

GroupFormulaExample
AlkenesC=CEthene
AlkynesC triple bond CEthyne
Alkyl halidesR-XChloroethane
AminesR-NH2Methyl amine
AmidesRCONH2Ethanamide
EthersR-O-R'Diethyl ether
AlcoholsR-OHMethanol
KetonesR-CO-R'Butanone
AldehydesR-CHOEthanal
Carboxylic acidsR-COOHEthanoic acid
EstersR-COO-R'Ethyl butanoate

Groups are divided as: having double/triple bonds; having C, H and halogens; having C, H and N; and having C, H and O. Acetic acid contains the carboxyl group -COOH.

Key Points

  • Functional group determines the properties and reactivity of a compound.
  • Alcohols are R-OH, carboxylic acids R-COOH, ethers R-O-R'.
  • Alkenes have a double bond, alkynes a triple bond.
  • Esters give fruits their distinct fragrance.

mcqs.q: A functional group is:
options: The longest carbon chain in the molecule
The group of atoms upon which the functions or properties of an organic compound depend; it is the most reactive part of the compound
Any hydrogen atom attached to carbon
The group that makes a compound inorganic
mcqs.why: A functional group is the group of atom(s) upon which the functions or properties of an organic compound depend. It is the most reactive part of the compound.

mcqs.q: Compounds having the same functional group:
options: Always have the same boiling point
Are always isomers of each other
Form the same homologous series and have the same chemical properties
mcqs.why: Compounds with the same functional group form the same homologous series, with the same chemical properties. This is why functional groups are used to classify organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Alcohols have the general form R-OH; the example given in the table is:
mcqs.why: In the functional group table, alcohols are R-OH with example methanol. Ethanal is an aldehyde (R-CHO), diethyl ether an ether (R-O-R') and ethanoic acid a carboxylic acid (R-COOH).

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids have the group R-COOH; acetic acid contains the:
mcqs.why: Acetic acid contains the carboxyl group -COOH. Carboxylic acids are R-COOH, e.g. ethanoic acid, while amides are RCONH2, e.g. ethanamide.

mcqs.q: Ethers have the general form:
mcqs.why: Ethers are R-O-R' with example diethyl ether. Alkyl halides are R-X (chloroethane) and amines are R-NH2 (methyl amine).

mcqs.q: Ethanal and butanone are examples of:
options: An aldehyde (R-CHO) and a ketone (R-CO-R') respectively
mcqs.why: Aldehydes are R-CHO, e.g. ethanal, and ketones are R-CO-R', e.g. butanone. Both contain a carbonyl group but in different positions.

mcqs.q: The distinct fragrance of fruits is due to the:
options: Ester group; banana has isopentyl acetate and orange has octyl acetate
mcqs.why: Fruit fragrance is due to the ester group: banana has isopentyl acetate, apple methyl butyrate and orange octyl acetate. Esters are R-COO-R', e.g. ethyl butanoate.

mcqs.q: Alkenes and alkynes are identified by their functional groups:
options: Alkenes have a C=C double bond (e.g. ethene) and alkynes a C triple bond (e.g. ethyne)
Alkenes have a triple bond and alkynes a double bond
mcqs.why: In the table, alkenes are C=C with example ethene, and alkynes have a carbon-carbon triple bond with example ethyne. Groups are divided as: having double/triple bonds; with halogens; with N; and with O.

mcqs.q: Chloroethane is an example of:
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides are R-X, e.g. chloroethane, where X is a halogen. Methyl amine is an amine R-NH2 and ethanamide is an amide RCONH2.

mcqs.q: Methyl amine, CH3-NH2 type, belongs to the functional group class of:
mcqs.why: Amines are R-NH2 with example methyl amine. Amides are RCONH2 (ethanamide) — the extra carbonyl carbon makes an amide different from an amine.

lessons.title: 12.1 Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
What are Hydrocarbons?

Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. They are the simplest organic compounds and the parent compounds of all other organic compounds. They occur in petroleum, natural gas and coal, formed from dead plants and animals buried under the earth millions of years ago. They are mostly used as fuels.

Classification

  • Open chain (aliphatic) compounds: carbon atoms form a chain, e.g. n-butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched chain).
  • Closed chain (cyclic) compounds: carbons form a ring. Alicyclic, e.g. cyclobutane, have properties like aliphatic compounds. Aromatic, e.g. benzene, have a ring of alternate single and double bonds.
  • Saturated hydrocarbons have only single bonds, e.g. ethane. Unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, e.g. ethene and ethyne.

Carbon atoms are primary (joined to 1 carbon), secondary (2 carbons), tertiary (3 carbons) or quaternary (4 carbons).

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain only C and H and come from petroleum, natural gas and coal.
  • Two main classes: open chain (aliphatic) and closed chain (cyclic).
  • Cyclic compounds are alicyclic or aromatic (e.g. benzene).
  • Single bonds = saturated; double/triple bonds = unsaturated.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons are called the parent compounds of all other organic compounds because they:
options: Contain only carbon and hydrogen and are the simplest organic compounds
Are found in every living cell
Have the largest molecules in chemistry
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. They are the simplest organic compounds and the parent compounds of all other organic compounds, occurring in petroleum, natural gas and coal.

mcqs.q: Open chain (aliphatic) hydrocarbons are those in which:
options: Carbon atoms form a closed ring
Carbon atoms form a chain, e.g. n-butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched chain)
Carbon atoms are joined to nitrogen atoms
Only one carbon atom is present
mcqs.why: Open chain compounds have carbons in a chain: n-butane is straight chain and 2-methylpropane is branched chain. Closed chain (cyclic) compounds have carbons forming a ring.

mcqs.q: Benzene is an example of an aromatic compound because it has:
options: A straight chain of six carbons
Only single bonds in a ring
A ring of alternate single and double bonds
A triple bond in its ring
mcqs.why: Closed chain compounds are alicyclic, e.g. cyclobutane, or aromatic, e.g. benzene, which has a ring of alternate single and double bonds.

mcqs.q: Saturated hydrocarbons are those having:
options: At least one double bond, e.g. ethene
At least one triple bond, e.g. ethyne
Both a ring and a triple bond
mcqs.why: Saturated hydrocarbons have only single bonds, e.g. ethane. Unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, e.g. ethene and ethyne.

mcqs.q: Alicyclic compounds, e.g. cyclobutane, have properties similar to:
mcqs.why: Alicyclic compounds such as cyclobutane are cyclic but have properties like aliphatic compounds, unlike aromatic compounds such as benzene with alternate bonds.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons found in petroleum, natural gas and coal were formed from:
options: Rocks melted deep inside the earth
Dead plants and animals buried under the earth millions of years ago
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons occur in petroleum, natural gas and coal, formed from dead plants and animals buried under the earth millions of years ago, and they are mostly used as fuels.

mcqs.q: A carbon atom joined to two other carbon atoms is called:
mcqs.why: Carbon atoms are primary (joined to 1 carbon), secondary (2 carbons), tertiary (3 carbons) or quaternary (4 carbons).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
options: Ethane, which has only single bonds
Ethene, which has a double bond
mcqs.why: Unsaturated hydrocarbons have double or triple bonds, e.g. ethene and ethyne. Ethane, methane and propane have only single bonds and are saturated.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons are mostly used as:
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons occur in petroleum, natural gas and coal and are mostly used as fuels, since burning them releases large amounts of energy.

mcqs.q: 2-Methylpropane is an example of:
mcqs.why: Open chain compounds include n-butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched chain). Cyclic examples are cyclobutane (alicyclic) and benzene (aromatic).

lessons.title: 12.2 The Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkanes

Alkanes have only single bonds between carbon atoms. Carbon forms 4 bonds, so alkanes cannot add more atoms and are saturated compounds. General formula: CnH2n+2. Names end with suffix ane. They are insoluble in water, dissolve in non-polar solvents, are relatively inert, and are used as fuel and lubricating oil.

NameCarbonsFormula
Methane1CH4
Ethane2C2H6
Propane3C3H8
Butane4C4H10
Pentane5C5H12
Decane10C10H22

Methane, CH4, is the first member. It has a regular tetrahedral structure: H-C-H angle 109.5 degrees, C-C length 1.54 A (154 pm) and C-H length 1.10 A (110 pm). Alkanes are obtained from natural gas and petroleum by fractional distillation. Cyclic alkanes do not follow CnH2n+2.

Naming Alkanes (12.2.1)
