IUPAC naming uses a root name for the longest chain: 1 = Meth, 2 = Eth, 3 = Prop, 4 = But, 5 = Pent. Branches are named as radicals and numbered from the end giving the lowest number, e.g. 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane (common name neopentane).

Key Points

  • Alkanes: single bonds only, saturated, general formula CnH2n+2, suffix ane.
  • First ten members run methane to decane (C10H22).
  • Methane is tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5 degrees.
  • IUPAC name = branch position + branch name + longest-chain root + ane.

mcqs.q: Alkanes cannot add more atoms and are called saturated because:
options: They are fully dissolved in water
They have only single bonds between carbon atoms and each carbon forms 4 bonds
They contain the maximum amount of oxygen
They have double bonds that are fully occupied
mcqs.why: Alkanes have only single bonds between carbon atoms. Carbon forms 4 bonds, so alkanes cannot add more atoms and are saturated compounds, with general formula CnH2n+2 and suffix ane.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n+2, the formula of pentane (5 carbons) is:
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 5, H = 2n + 2 = 2(5) + 2 = 12, so pentane is C5H12. The table runs methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, pentane C5H12 and decane C10H22.

mcqs.q: Methane, CH4, has a regular tetrahedral structure with H-C-H bond angle of:
mcqs.why: Methane is the first member of the alkanes. It has a regular tetrahedral structure: H-C-H angle 109.5 degrees, C-C length 1.54 A (154 pm) and C-H length 1.10 A (110 pm).

mcqs.q: In alkanes, the C-C bond length and C-H bond length are respectively:
mcqs.why: From the structure of methane: C-C length is 1.54 A (154 pm) and C-H length is 1.10 A (110 pm), with the tetrahedral H-C-H angle of 109.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are obtained from natural gas and petroleum by:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are obtained from natural gas and petroleum by fractional distillation. They are insoluble in water, dissolve in non-polar solvents, are relatively inert, and are used as fuel and lubricating oil.

mcqs.q: Cyclic alkanes are an exception because they:
options: Have no carbon atoms in a ring
Do not follow the general formula CnH2n+2
mcqs.why: The notes state that cyclic alkanes do not follow CnH2n+2, because forming a ring removes two hydrogens compared with the open chain alkane of the same carbon number.

mcqs.q: In IUPAC naming of alkanes, the root name for a chain of 5 carbon atoms is:
options: Pent, so the alkane is pentane
mcqs.why: IUPAC naming uses a root name for the longest chain: 1 = Meth, 2 = Eth, 3 = Prop, 4 = But, 5 = Pent. Branches are named as radicals and numbered from the end giving the lowest number.

mcqs.q: The common name of 2,2-dimethylpropane is:
mcqs.why: Branches are numbered from the end giving the lowest number, e.g. 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane, whose common name is neopentane.

mcqs.q: Decane, the alkane with 10 carbon atoms, has the formula:
mcqs.why: From CnH2n+2 with n = 10: H = 2(10) + 2 = 22, so decane is C10H22. The first ten members run from methane to decane.

mcqs.q: Alkanes dissolve in:
options: Non-polar solvents, being insoluble in water
mcqs.why: Alkanes are insoluble in water, dissolve in non-polar solvents, are relatively inert, and are used as fuel and lubricating oil. Their names end with the suffix ane.

lessons.title: 12.2.2 Preparation of Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Alkanes (12.2.2)

1. Hydrogenation: addition of hydrogen to alkenes and alkynes in presence of Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst gives alkanes. Ethene + H2 -> ethane (Ni, 250-300 C). Ethyne is hydrogenated in two steps: ethyne -> ethene -> ethane.

2. Reduction of alkyl halides: alkyl halides are reduced with Zn/HCl at room temperature, e.g. ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl.

Physical Properties (12.2.3)

Alkanes are covalent, non-polar compounds. Melting and boiling points increase with carbon number. First four members are gases, from 5 carbons they are liquids, and above 20 carbons they are waxy solids. They dissolve in non-polar solvents like benzene.

Chemical Properties (12.2.4)

Alkanes are less reactive, so they are called paraffins. Halogenation: in light, Cl2 replaces H atoms step by step: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, then CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and finally CCl4. Combustion: complete oxidation gives CO2 and water with much energy: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, 890 KJ/mole; propane gives 2219 KJ/mole.

Key Points

  • Alkanes are prepared by hydrogenation (Ni/Pd) and by reduction of alkyl halides (Zn/HCl).
  • C1-C4 are gases, C5 onwards liquids, above C20 waxy solids.
  • Halogenation in light replaces H by Cl one by one up to CCl4.
  • Combustion of methane releases 890 KJ/mole.

mcqs.q: Alkanes can be prepared by hydrogenation, which is:
options: Removal of hydrogen from alkanes by heating
Addition of hydrogen to alkenes and alkynes in the presence of a Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst
Reaction of alkanes with chlorine in light
mcqs.why: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen to alkenes and alkynes in presence of Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst to give alkanes: ethene + H2 -> ethane (Ni, 250-300 C).

mcqs.q: Ethyne is hydrogenated to ethane in:
options: One step directly, with no intermediate
mcqs.why: Ethyne is hydrogenated in two steps: ethyne -> ethene -> ethane, because the triple bond is first reduced to a double bond and then to a single bond.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides are reduced to alkanes using:
options: Zn/HCl at room temperature, e.g. ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl
mcqs.why: Reduction of alkyl halides: alkyl halides are reduced with Zn/HCl at room temperature, e.g. ethyl chloride + 2[H] -> ethane + HCl.

mcqs.q: The first four members of the alkanes are gases; from 5 carbons onwards they are:
options: Liquids, and above 20 carbons they are waxy solids
mcqs.why: Alkanes are covalent, non-polar compounds whose melting and boiling points increase with carbon number: C1-C4 are gases, from 5 carbons they are liquids, and above 20 carbons they are waxy solids.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are called paraffins because they are:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are less reactive, so they are called paraffins. Their main reactions are halogenation in light and combustion, which gives CO2 and water with much energy.

mcqs.q: In the halogenation of methane in light, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms:
options: All at once, giving CCl4 directly with no intermediates
Only once, giving CH3Cl as the final product
In the dark, without any light
Step by step: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, then CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and finally CCl4
mcqs.why: Halogenation: in light, Cl2 replaces H atoms step by step: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl, then CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and finally CCl4. Light is essential for this substitution.

mcqs.q: According to this lesson, the combustion of one mole of methane releases:
mcqs.why: Combustion: complete oxidation gives CO2 and water with much energy: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, 890 KJ/mole; propane gives 2219 KJ/mole, as stated in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Ethene is converted into ethane by hydrogenation using a nickel catalyst at:
mcqs.why: Ethene + H2 -> ethane takes place with Ni at 250-300 C. Ni, Pt or Pd can all catalyse the hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes.

mcqs.q: Alkanes dissolve in non-polar solvents such as:
mcqs.why: Alkanes are covalent, non-polar compounds. They dissolve in non-polar solvents like benzene, and their melting and boiling points increase with carbon number.

mcqs.q: The complete combustion of an alkane always produces:
options: Carbon dioxide and water, with a large amount of energy
mcqs.why: Combustion is complete oxidation giving CO2 and water with much energy, e.g. CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O releasing 890 KJ/mole. This is why alkanes are used as fuels.

lessons.title: 12.3 The Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkenes

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one double bond. General formula: CnH2n (for one double bond). Suffix ane is replaced by ene. Examples: ethene H2C=CH2, propene CH2=CH-CH3, 1-butene and 2-butene. They are more reactive than alkanes and are used as starting material for many organic compounds. They are also called olefins (oil-forming).

Preparation (12.3.1)

  • Dehydration of alcohols: ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170 C gives ethene: CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O.
  • Dehydrohalogenation: removing HX from alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH at 100 C, e.g. ethyl bromide -> ethene + KBr + H2O.

Reactions and Uses (12.3.2)

  • Addition of halogens: at room temperature in CCl4, e.g. propene + Cl2 -> dichloropropane.
  • Hydrohalogenation: CH2=CH2 + HBr -> ethyl bromide; used to prepare alkyl halides.
  • Oxidation: 1% alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) gives glycols and its pink colour is discharged - a test for a double bond.

Uses: making polythene, glycols, alcohols and halogen derivatives. Hydrogenation of alkenes makes ghee. Ethene is used for polythene plastic, ripening fruits and as a general anaesthetic.

Key Points

  • Alkenes: at least one double bond, general formula CnH2n, suffix ene.
  • Prepared by dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides.
  • They give addition reactions; KMnO4 pink colour is discharged (Baeyer test).
  • Ethene is used for polythene and for ripening fruits.

mcqs.q: The general formula of alkenes (with one double bond) is:
mcqs.why: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one double bond, general formula CnH2n for one double bond, and the suffix ane is replaced by ene. Examples: ethene, propene, 1-butene and 2-butene.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n, the formula of butene (4 carbons) is:
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 4, H = 2n = 2 x 4 = 8, so butene is C4H8. Compare alkanes CnH2n+2 (butane C4H10) and alkynes CnH2n-2 (butyne C4H6).

mcqs.q: Alkenes are also called olefins, which means:
mcqs.why: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and are used as starting material for many organic compounds. They are also called olefins, meaning oil-forming.

mcqs.q: Ethene is prepared by the dehydration of ethanol using:
options: Concentrated H2SO4 at 170 C: CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O
mcqs.why: Dehydration of alcohols: ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170 C gives ethene: CH3CH2OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O. Water is removed from the alcohol to form the double bond.

mcqs.q: Dehydrohalogenation is the removal of HX from an alkyl halide using:
options: Alcoholic KOH at 100 C, e.g. ethyl bromide -> ethene + KBr + H2O
mcqs.why: Dehydrohalogenation: removing HX from alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH at 100 C, e.g. ethyl bromide -> ethene + KBr + H2O. Zn/HCl instead reduces alkyl halides to alkanes.

mcqs.q: The Baeyer test for a double bond uses 1% alkaline KMnO4, in which:
options: The pink colour of KMnO4 is discharged and a glycol is formed
A brick red precipitate is formed
mcqs.why: Oxidation: 1% alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) gives glycols and its pink colour is discharged — this is the standard test for a double bond in alkenes.

mcqs.q: Hydrohalogenation of ethene with HBr gives:
mcqs.why: Hydrohalogenation: CH2=CH2 + HBr -> ethyl bromide. This addition reaction is used to prepare alkyl halides from alkenes.

mcqs.q: Addition of chlorine to propene in CCl4 at room temperature gives:
mcqs.why: Addition of halogens takes place at room temperature in CCl4, e.g. propene + Cl2 -> dichloropropane: the two chlorine atoms add across the double bond.

mcqs.q: Ethene is used for:
options: Making polythene, ripening fruits and as a general anaesthetic
mcqs.why: Uses of ethene: making polythene plastic, ripening fruits and as a general anaesthetic. Alkenes are also used for making glycols, alcohols and halogen derivatives, and their hydrogenation makes ghee.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of their:
options: Double bond, across which addition reactions take place
mcqs.why: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one double bond, so they give addition reactions (of halogens, HBr, hydrogen) and are more reactive than the saturated alkanes.

lessons.title: 12.4 The Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
The Alkynes

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one triple bond, so they are more unsaturated than alkenes. General formula: CnH2n-2, suffix yne. Examples: ethyne (acetylene) HC=CH in triple bond form C2H2, propyne and 1-butyne. Acetylene burns with oxygen at very high temperature: 2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O + heat, so it is used in oxy-acetylene torches for cutting and welding metals.

Preparation (12.4.1)

  • Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides: halogens on adjacent carbons are removed with alcoholic KOH, e.g. vicinal dibromide + 2KOH -> ethyne + 2KBr + 2H2O.
  • Dehalogenation of tetrahalides: with Zn dust, e.g. 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn -> ethyne + 2ZnBr2.

Properties, Reactions and Uses

First members are gases; boiling and melting points rise with chain length and are higher than corresponding alkenes. They are non-polar, insoluble in water, and dissolve in benzene and ether. Alkynes are reactive but generally less reactive than alkenes. Addition of halogens: ethyne + 2Cl2 -> 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane at room temperature. Oxidation: KMnO4 in acid breaks the triple bond: ethyne + 4[O] -> oxalic acid; this locates the triple bond. Uses: starting material for PVC, synthetic rubber, alcohols and alkyl halides; acetylene is used for welding and artificial ripening of fruits like mangoes. Calcium carbide gives acetylene with water: CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2.

Key Points

  • Alkynes: at least one triple bond, general formula CnH2n-2, suffix yne.
  • Prepared from vicinal dihalides (alcoholic KOH) and tetrahalides (Zn dust).
  • Ethyne + Cl2 gives tetrachloroethane; KMnO4 oxidation gives oxalic acid.
  • Acetylene is used in oxy-acetylene welding and fruit ripening.

mcqs.q: The general formula of alkynes is:
mcqs.why: Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one triple bond, general formula CnH2n-2, with suffix yne. Examples: ethyne (acetylene) C2H2, propyne and 1-butyne.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n-2, the formula of propyne (3 carbons) is:
mcqs.why: Working: for n = 3, H = 2n - 2 = 2(3) - 2 = 4, so propyne is C3H4. Compare propane C3H8 (alkane) and propene C3H6 (alkene).

mcqs.q: Ethyne is commonly known as:
mcqs.why: Ethyne (acetylene) is HC=CH in triple bond form, C2H2. It burns with oxygen at very high temperature, so it is used in oxy-acetylene torches for cutting and welding metals.

mcqs.q: The oxy-acetylene flame is based on the reaction:
mcqs.why: Acetylene burns with oxygen at very high temperature: 2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O + heat, so it is used in oxy-acetylene torches for cutting and welding metals.

mcqs.q: Alkynes are prepared from vicinal dihalides by dehydrohalogenation using:
options: Alcoholic KOH, e.g. vicinal dibromide + 2KOH -> ethyne + 2KBr + 2H2O
mcqs.why: Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides: halogens on adjacent carbons are removed with alcoholic KOH, e.g. vicinal dibromide + 2KOH -> ethyne + 2KBr + 2H2O.

mcqs.q: Dehalogenation of tetrahalides to give alkynes is carried out with:
mcqs.why: Dehalogenation of tetrahalides is done with Zn dust: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn -> ethyne + 2ZnBr2. Zn removes the halogen atoms, forming the triple bond.

mcqs.q: Addition of chlorine to ethyne gives:
mcqs.why: Addition of halogens: ethyne + 2Cl2 -> 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane at room temperature. Two molecules of Cl2 add across the triple bond in two steps.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of ethyne with KMnO4 in acid gives oxalic acid, and this reaction is used to:
options: Locate the position of the triple bond
mcqs.why: Oxidation: KMnO4 in acid breaks the triple bond: ethyne + 4[O] -> oxalic acid; this locates the triple bond. The Baeyer test with alkaline KMnO4 is for double bonds.

mcqs.q: Calcium carbide reacts with water to give acetylene:
mcqs.why: Calcium carbide gives acetylene with water: CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. This is a convenient laboratory preparation of ethyne.

mcqs.q: Compared with alkenes, alkynes are generally:
options: Less reactive, though both are unsaturated; alkynes are non-polar and insoluble in water
mcqs.why: Alkynes are reactive but generally less reactive than alkenes. They are non-polar, insoluble in water, and dissolve in benzene and ether; their first members are gases.

lessons.title: 13.1 Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Biochemistry studies compounds in living organisms: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and vitamins.

What are Carbohydrates?

Carbohydrates are the most abundant bio-compounds, used mostly as a source of energy. General formula Cx(H2O)y, so called hydrates of carbon. Glucose is C6H12O6; sucrose, C12H22O11, does not fit. They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones: many -OH groups with -CHO (glucose) or a ketonic group (fructose). Made by photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (chlorophyll, sunlight).

Classification

  • Monosaccharides (1 unit): white, water-soluble, crystalline, sweet; building blocks of the others. First member glyceraldehyde, C3H6O3, has three carbons. Others: glucose, fructose (fruit sugar), galactose, ribose C5H10O5.
  • Oligosaccharides (2-10 units, loss of water): sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose.
  • Polysaccharides (more than 10): starch, glycogen, cellulose - all glucose units, differing in sequence.

Sources and Uses

CarbohydrateSource
GlucoseGrapes
FructoseFruits, honey
SucroseSugar cane, beet root
LactoseMilk and dairy products
StarchPotato, cereals like wheat, rice, maize
GlycogenAnimal liver

Plants store starch, animals glycogen; cellulose makes cell walls. Uses: building, paper, cotton clothing, 5% glucose drips.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates have general formula Cx(H2O)y and give instant energy.
  • They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, made by photosynthesis.
  • Classes differ by sugar units: mono 1, oligo 2-10, poly more than 10.
  • Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides of glucose.

mcqs.q: Carbohydrates are called hydrates of carbon because their general formula is:
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are the most abundant bio-compounds with general formula Cx(H2O)y, so they are called hydrates of carbon. Glucose is C6H12O6, while sucrose C12H22O11 does not fit the formula.

mcqs.q: Carbohydrates are chemically defined as:
options: Polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones: many -OH groups with -CHO (glucose) or a ketonic group (fructose)
Esters of fatty acids and glycerol
Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones: many -OH groups with -CHO (glucose) or a ketonic group (fructose). They are made by photosynthesis in plants.

mcqs.q: The photosynthesis reaction that produces glucose is:
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are made by photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, taking place in chlorophyll in the presence of sunlight.

mcqs.q: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates; they are:
options: Made of more than 10 sugar units
Single-unit sugars: white, water-soluble, crystalline and sweet, e.g. glucose, fructose, galactose and ribose
mcqs.why: Monosaccharides (1 unit) are white, water-soluble, crystalline and sweet, and are the building blocks of the others. The first member glyceraldehyde, C3H6O3, has three carbons.

mcqs.q: Sucrose is an oligosaccharide made of:
mcqs.why: Oligosaccharides (2-10 units, with loss of water): sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose and maltose = glucose + glucose.

mcqs.q: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides, and all three are made of:
options: Glucose units only, differing in their sequence
mcqs.why: Polysaccharides (more than 10 units): starch, glycogen and cellulose are all glucose units, differing in sequence. Plants store starch, animals store glycogen, and cellulose makes cell walls.

mcqs.q: Lactose, the sugar of milk and dairy products, is formed from:
mcqs.why: Lactose = glucose + galactose, and its source is milk and dairy products. Maltose is glucose + glucose and sucrose is glucose + fructose.

mcqs.q: Which carbohydrate is stored in the animal liver?
mcqs.why: From the sources table: glycogen is found in animal liver, glucose in grapes, fructose in fruits and honey, sucrose in sugar cane and beet root, and starch in potato and cereals.

mcqs.q: Plants store carbohydrates as starch, while animals store them as:
mcqs.why: Plants store starch and animals store glycogen; cellulose makes the cell walls of plants. All three are polysaccharides built from glucose units.

mcqs.q: A 5% glucose drip given to patients is an example of the use of carbohydrates in:
options: Medicine, as an instant energy source
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are used mostly as a source of energy: uses include building, paper, cotton clothing and 5% glucose drips, which supply instant energy to patients.

lessons.title: 13.2 Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are giant bio-organic compounds formed by joining amino acids. From Greek proteios (first); vital to every cell.

Roles in the Body

  • As skin, hair, cartilage, muscles, tendons and ligaments, they hold together, protect and give structure.
  • As enzymes, hormones, antibodies and globulins, they catalyse, regulate and protect body chemistry.
  • As haemoglobin, myoglobin and lipoproteins, they transport oxygen and other substances.

13.2.1 Amino Acids as Building Blocks

An amino acid has both an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH in one molecule, on a central carbon with H and an R (alkyl) chain. Human proteins use 20 different amino acids: 10 are made by the body and the remaining 10 essential amino acids must be taken in food. When amino acids join, a water molecule is eliminated and the joining bond is a peptide bond. Thousands linked by peptide bonds form a protein, which folds to save space; on hydrolysis a protein gives back its amino acids.

13.2.2 Sources and Uses

Protein is the basic body stuff; the dry mass of animals is about 50% protein. Plants make their own protein, animals mostly take amino acids in food. Sources: meat, eggs, beans, lentils, pulses, dry fruits and seeds.

  • Main stuff of the body, present in almost every tissue.
  • Act as carriers of substances in the body.
  • Act as catalysts (enzymes) - without them body functions stop; also serve as hormones.
  • Leather, a protein, is used for shoes, clothes and sports articles.

Key Points

  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
  • Each amino acid has -NH2 and -COOH groups and an R chain.
  • Of 20 amino acids, 10 are essential and must come from food.
  • Proteins build the body and work as enzymes, hormones and carriers.

mcqs.q: Proteins are giant bio-organic compounds formed by joining:
mcqs.why: Proteins are formed by joining amino acids. The word comes from Greek proteios (first), and proteins are vital to every cell of the body.

mcqs.q: Every amino acid contains, in one molecule:
options: An amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH, on a central carbon with H and an R (alkyl) chain
A phosphate group and a sugar
mcqs.why: An amino acid has both an amino group -NH2 and a carboxyl group -COOH in one molecule, on a central carbon with H and an R (alkyl) chain.

mcqs.q: Human proteins use 20 different amino acids, of which the essential ones that must be taken in food number:
mcqs.why: Human proteins use 20 different amino acids: 10 are made by the body and the remaining 10 essential amino acids must be taken in food, from sources like meat, eggs, beans and lentils.

mcqs.q: When amino acids join to form a protein, a water molecule is eliminated and the joining bond is called a:
mcqs.why: When amino acids join, a water molecule is eliminated and the joining bond is a peptide bond. Thousands of amino acids linked by peptide bonds form a protein.

mcqs.q: On hydrolysis, a protein gives back:
mcqs.why: A protein folds to save space, and on hydrolysis a protein gives back its amino acids, reversing the joining that formed the peptide bonds.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of the dry mass of animals is protein?
mcqs.why: Protein is the basic body stuff; the dry mass of animals is about 50% protein. Plants make their own protein, while animals mostly take amino acids in food.

mcqs.q: In the body, haemoglobin and myoglobin are proteins that work as:
options: Carriers that transport oxygen and other substances
mcqs.why: As haemoglobin, myoglobin and lipoproteins, proteins transport oxygen and other substances. As enzymes, hormones, antibodies and globulins, they catalyse, regulate and protect body chemistry.

mcqs.q: Enzymes, which catalyse body reactions, are chemically:
mcqs.why: Proteins act as catalysts (enzymes) — without them body functions stop; they also serve as hormones, and as skin, hair, cartilage, muscles, tendons and ligaments they give structure and protection.

mcqs.q: Rich food sources of proteins include:
options: Sugar cane, beet root and honey
Meat, eggs, beans, lentils, pulses, dry fruits and seeds
mcqs.why: Sources of protein: meat, eggs, beans, lentils, pulses, dry fruits and seeds. Protein is the main stuff of the body, present in almost every tissue.

mcqs.q: Leather, used for shoes, clothes and sports articles, is chemically a:
mcqs.why: Leather, a protein, is used for shoes, clothes and sports articles. This is one of the uses of proteins besides building the body and working as enzymes, hormones and carriers.

lessons.title: 13.3 Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol (glycerine). Members include fats, steroids, terpenes and waxes. Fats are triesters of glycerol and long-chained carboxylic acids (alkyl chains R1, R2, R3), yield a lot of energy, and are taken as animal fat, margarine, butter and cream. Oils are unsaturated, liquid at normal temperature, usually in plant products.

Steroids and Waxes

Steroids have a characteristic four condensed rings structure. They act as hormones, e.g. male and female sex hormones testosterone and progesterone, and steroidal compounds in bile juices help digestion. Waxes coat leaves and stems and prevent plants losing excessive water, e.g. Corunda wax on Brazilian palm leaves, used in floor and automobile waxes; lanolin coats lambs wool. Waxes give lubrication, protection and energy storage, and are used in ointments, hand creams and cosmetics.

13.3.1 Fatty Acids

Fatty acids are the bio-organic compounds that form lipids: carboxylic acids with a -COOH group and a long chain of unbranched carbons as a tail, e.g. palmitic acid (C15H31COOH) and stearic acid (C17H35COOH).

13.3.2 Sources and Uses of Lipids

In animals lipids are found as fats and in milk; in plants as oils. They are a source of large energy, increase the taste of food (butter, ghee, oils), are used as stored fat by hibernating animals, and fatty tissues protect humans and animals from severe cold. Oily layers protect desert plants from transpiration. Many oils and fats are used as drugs, e.g. cod liver oil.

Key Points

  • Lipids are long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Fats are solid diet lipids; oils are unsaturated and liquid at normal temperature.
  • Steroids have four condensed rings and act as hormones.
  • Lipids store large energy and insulate the body against cold.

options: Long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol (glycerine)
Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen
mcqs.why: Lipids are long-chained esters of fatty acids and glycerol. Members include fats, steroids, terpenes and waxes; fats are triesters of glycerol and long-chained carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Oils differ from fats because oils are:
options: Saturated and solid at normal temperature
Unsaturated and liquid at normal temperature, usually found in plant products
mcqs.why: Fats are solid diet lipids, while oils are unsaturated, liquid at normal temperature and usually in plant products. Both are taken as animal fat, margarine, butter and cream type foods.

mcqs.q: Steroids, such as the sex hormones testosterone and progesterone, have a characteristic structure of:
options: A single ring with a side chain
mcqs.why: Steroids have a characteristic four condensed rings structure. They act as hormones, e.g. male and female sex hormones testosterone and progesterone, and steroidal compounds in bile juices help digestion.

mcqs.q: Waxes coat the leaves and stems of plants in order to:
options: Prevent the plants from losing excessive water
mcqs.why: Waxes coat leaves and stems and prevent plants losing excessive water, e.g. Corunda wax on Brazilian palm leaves; lanolin coats lambs wool. Waxes are used in floor and automobile waxes, ointments and cosmetics.

mcqs.q: Fatty acids, the building units of lipids, are:
options: Carboxylic acids with a -COOH group and a long unbranched carbon chain as a tail, e.g. palmitic acid C15H31COOH
mcqs.why: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with a -COOH group and a long chain of unbranched carbons as a tail, e.g. palmitic acid (C15H31COOH) and stearic acid (C17H35COOH).

mcqs.q: Stearic acid, a common fatty acid, has the formula:
mcqs.why: The two examples given are palmitic acid (C15H31COOH) and stearic acid (C17H35COOH). Both are long-chained carboxylic acids that form lipids with glycerol.

mcqs.q: Hibernating animals survive the winter using lipids because lipids:
options: Are stored as fat and yield a lot of energy
Keep the body warm by producing light
Act as hormones in the body
mcqs.why: Lipids are a source of large energy, are used as stored fat by hibernating animals, and fatty tissues protect humans and animals from severe cold.

mcqs.why: Lipids store large energy and insulate the body against cold; oily layers also protect desert plants from transpiration. Many oils and fats are used as drugs, e.g. cod liver oil.

mcqs.why: Many oils and fats are used as drugs, e.g. cod liver oil. In animals lipids are found as fats and in milk; in plants as oils.

mcqs.q: Fats are triesters formed from:
options: Glycerol and one fatty acid only
Glycerol and three long-chained carboxylic acids (fatty acids), with alkyl chains R1, R2, R3
mcqs.why: Fats are triesters of glycerol and long-chained carboxylic acids (alkyl chains R1, R2, R3). They yield a lot of energy and are taken as animal fat, margarine, butter and cream.

lessons.title: 13.4 Nucleic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are the special biopolymers responsible for heredity. There are two types: DNA (Deoxyribose nucleic acid) and RNA (Ribose nucleic acid). They carry genetic information in the sequence of their subunits, called nucleotides. A nucleotide directs production of a specific protein, and these proteins run the cells, so the body acts under the command of DNA and RNA built genes. Small differences in DNA sequences cause the diversity of life; the genetic material of humans and chimpanzees differs by only 3%.

13.4.1 DNA

DNA gives us our identity and controls cell functioning; its instructions make each tissue behave separately. Its complicated structure was discovered by J-Watson and F-Crick in 1953. Each nucleotide is made of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. DNA has 4 bases: Adenine, Cytosine, Thiamine and Guanine (A, T, C, G). Their sequence forms the code of DNA; each gene has its distinct code. Two strands run parallel, so DNA is a double-stranded giant structure.

13.4.2 RNA

RNA is the second type, like DNA but single-stranded. Its nucleotide also has 3 basic groups, with two differences: its pentose sugar is ribose instead of deoxyribose, and the base uracil replaces thiamine. RNA carries messages from DNA, forms different proteins on the command of DNA, and these proteins catalyse and control cell reactions and processes. In a DNA test, the characteristic sequence inherited from parents is matched.

Key Points

  • Nucleic acids are of two types: DNA and RNA, the units of heredity.
  • A nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base.
  • DNA is double-stranded, with bases A, T, C and G; its structure was given by Watson and Crick in 1953.
  • RNA is single-stranded, has ribose sugar and uracil instead of thiamine.

mcqs.q: Nucleic acids are the biopolymers responsible for:
options: Providing instant energy to the body
Heredity, carrying genetic information in the sequence of their nucleotides
mcqs.why: Nucleic acids are the special biopolymers responsible for heredity. They carry genetic information in the sequence of their subunits, called nucleotides.

mcqs.q: The two types of nucleic acids are:
options: DNA (deoxyribose nucleic acid) and RNA (ribose nucleic acid)
mcqs.why: There are two types: DNA (Deoxyribose nucleic acid) and RNA (Ribose nucleic acid). Small differences in DNA sequences cause the diversity of life.

mcqs.q: A nucleotide, the subunit of nucleic acids, is made of:
options: An amino group, a carboxyl group and an R chain
A phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A fatty acid, glycerol and a phosphate group
mcqs.why: Each nucleotide is made of a phosphate group, a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base. A nucleotide directs production of a specific protein.

mcqs.q: The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953 by:
mcqs.why: The complicated structure of DNA was discovered by J-Watson and F-Crick in 1953. DNA is a double-stranded giant structure whose base sequence forms the genetic code.

mcqs.q: The four nitrogenous bases in DNA are:
options: Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine and Guanine (A, T, C, G)
mcqs.why: DNA has 4 bases: Adenine, Cytosine, Thymine and Guanine (A, T, C, G), as printed in the notes. In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.

mcqs.q: RNA differs from DNA because RNA:
options: Is single-stranded, has ribose sugar, and has uracil instead of thymine
Is double-stranded and has deoxyribose sugar
mcqs.why: RNA is single-stranded; its pentose sugar is ribose instead of deoxyribose, and the base uracil replaces thymine. RNA carries messages from DNA and forms different proteins on the command of DNA.

mcqs.q: The genetic material of humans and chimpanzees differs by only:
mcqs.why: Small differences in DNA sequences cause the diversity of life; the genetic material of humans and chimpanzees differs by only 3%.

mcqs.q: DNA gives us our identity and its instructions make each tissue behave separately; this is because DNA:
options: Controls cell functioning through its distinct gene codes
mcqs.why: DNA gives us our identity and controls cell functioning; its instructions make each tissue behave separately, and each gene has its distinct code in the sequence of bases.

mcqs.q: In a DNA test, identification is done by matching:
options: The blood group of the person
The amount of protein in the blood
The characteristic sequence inherited from parents
mcqs.why: In a DNA test, the characteristic sequence inherited from parents is matched. The proteins made on the command of DNA catalyse and control cell reactions and processes.

mcqs.q: The sugar present in DNA nucleotides is:
mcqs.why: DNA is deoxyribose nucleic acid and RNA is ribose nucleic acid: DNA's pentose sugar is deoxyribose and RNA's is ribose, one of the two differences between them.

lessons.title: 13.5 Vitamins
lessons.notes_html:
Vitamins are organic compounds needed in the diet for normal body health. The name was given by Polish biochemist Kazimierz Funk in 1912, from Latin vita (life) and amin (amine). They are essential for normal growth and health, act as catalysts or co-enzymes, and prevent and cure many diseases.

13.5.1 Types of Vitamins

  • Water-soluble: vitamin-B and vitamin-C. Excreted in urine, so taken daily. Vitamin-B is a group (B1, B2, etc.).
  • Fat-soluble (water-insoluble): vitamin-A, D, E and K. Stored in body tissues, so not needed daily.
VitaminSolubilityDaily requirementDeficiency diseaseSources
Vitamin-AFat900 ugNight-blindnessAnimal tissues, especially fish and liver
Vitamin-BWater1.2-1.5 mgBeriberi, anemiaMeats, leafy green vegetables, grains, legumes
Vitamin-CWater90.0 mgScurvyCitrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes, leafy green vegetables
Vitamin-DFat5.0-10 ugRickets and OsteomalaciaSynthesized in skin in sunlight; fortified foods

13.5.2 Importance of Vitamins

Vitamins mostly play their role in metabolic pathways. Taken in increased amount, fat-soluble vitamins (e.g. vitamin-A) can cause disease - hypervitaminosis, whose common symptoms are nausea and vomiting.

Key Points

  • Vitamins are needed in small amounts for growth, health and metabolism.
  • Vitamin-B and C are water-soluble and are required daily.
  • Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are stored in the body.
  • Lack of A causes night-blindness, B causes beriberi, C causes scurvy and D causes rickets.

mcqs.q: The name 'vitamin' was given in 1912 by the Polish biochemist:
options: Kazimierz Funk, from Latin vita (life) and amin (amine)
mcqs.why: The name vitamin was given by Polish biochemist Kazimierz Funk in 1912, from Latin vita (life) and amin (amine). Vitamins are essential for normal growth and health.

mcqs.q: Water-soluble vitamins are:
options: Vitamin-B and vitamin-C; they are excreted in urine, so they must be taken daily
mcqs.why: Water-soluble vitamins are vitamin-B and vitamin-C; they are excreted in urine, so they are taken daily. Vitamin-B is a group (B1, B2, etc.).

mcqs.q: Fat-soluble vitamins, which are stored in body tissues and not needed daily, are:
mcqs.why: Fat-soluble (water-insoluble) vitamins are vitamin-A, D, E and K. They are stored in body tissues, so they are not needed daily, unlike the water-soluble B and C.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of vitamin-A (daily requirement 900 ug) causes:
mcqs.why: From the vitamin table: vitamin-A deficiency causes night-blindness; its sources are animal tissues, especially fish and liver. Vitamin-B deficiency causes beriberi, C causes scurvy and D causes rickets.

mcqs.q: Beriberi and anemia are deficiency diseases of:
mcqs.why: Vitamin-B (1.2-1.5 mg daily) has deficiency diseases beriberi and anemia; its sources are meats, leafy green vegetables, grains and legumes.

mcqs.q: Scurvy is caused by the deficiency of vitamin-C, whose rich sources are:
options: Citrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes and leafy green vegetables
mcqs.why: Vitamin-C (90.0 mg daily) deficiency causes scurvy; sources are citrus fruits, strawberries, tomatoes and leafy green vegetables. Vitamin-C is water-soluble and must be taken daily.

mcqs.q: Vitamin-D is special because it is:
options: Synthesized in the skin in sunlight; its deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia
mcqs.why: Vitamin-D (5.0-10 ug daily) is synthesized in skin in sunlight and also taken from fortified foods; its deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia. It is a fat-soluble vitamin.

mcqs.q: Hypervitaminosis is the disease condition caused by:
options: Deficiency of vitamin-C in the diet
Excess of water-soluble vitamins in food
Taking fat-soluble vitamins (e.g. vitamin-A) in increased amount; common symptoms are nausea and vomiting
mcqs.why: Taken in increased amount, fat-soluble vitamins (e.g. vitamin-A) can cause disease — hypervitaminosis, whose common symptoms are nausea and vomiting — because they are stored in body tissues.

mcqs.q: In the body, vitamins mostly play their role in metabolic pathways as:
mcqs.why: Vitamins are needed in small amounts for growth, health and metabolism; they act as catalysts or co-enzymes and prevent and cure many diseases, but they are not energy sources.

mcqs.q: Vitamin-B is not a single vitamin but:
options: A group of vitamins (B1, B2, etc.)
mcqs.why: Vitamin-B is a group (B1, B2, etc.). It is water-soluble, excreted in urine and required daily, with a daily requirement of 1.2-1.5 mg.

lessons.title: 14.1 Composition of the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
What is the Atmosphere?

The atmosphere is the layer of gases that covers our planet earth. This mixture of gases is commonly known as air. Compared with the diameter of the earth, the atmosphere is very thin and lasts up to about 500 km. It has no definite boundary; it slowly thins and finally fades into outer space.

Composition of Air

GasPercentage
Nitrogen78%
Oxygen (O2)20.95%
Argon0.93%
Carbon dioxide (CO2)0.04%
Water vapoursabout 1%
Other gasestrace amounts

Importance of the Atmosphere

  • All living things rely on air for normal life processes, e.g. respiration.
  • It serves as a thermo blanket which maintains a specific temperature for organisms.
  • Its coating of gases protects the earth and life from the hazardous radiation of space.
  • The constituents are present in different layers, each having a distinct character. Any change in composition could be fatal to all life forms, so it must be maintained as it is.

Key Points

  • Atmosphere is the layer of gases covering the earth, extending to about 500 km with no definite boundary.
  • Air contains 78% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.
  • About 1% water vapours are also an important part of the atmosphere.
  • It acts as a thermo blanket and protects life from hazardous space radiation.

mcqs.q: The atmosphere extends above the earth's surface up to about:
options: 500 km, thinning gradually with no definite boundary
mcqs.why: The atmosphere is the layer of gases covering the earth. Compared with the diameter of the earth it is very thin and lasts up to about 500 km; it has no definite boundary and slowly fades into outer space.

mcqs.q: The most abundant gas in air is nitrogen, which makes up:
mcqs.why: Composition of air: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 20.95%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.04%, water vapours about 1% and other gases in trace amounts.

mcqs.q: Oxygen forms what percentage of the air?
mcqs.why: Oxygen (O2) is 20.95% of air. Nitrogen is 78%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.04% and water vapours about 1%.

mcqs.q: In 10,000 parts of air, the number of parts of oxygen is:
mcqs.why: Working: oxygen is 20.95% of air, so in 10,000 parts there are 20.95/100 x 10,000 = 2,095 parts of oxygen. (Nitrogen would be 78/100 x 10,000 = 7,800 parts.)

mcqs.q: Argon and carbon dioxide form respectively what percentages of air?
mcqs.why: From the composition table: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 20.95%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.04% and water vapours about 1%, with other gases in trace amounts.

mcqs.q: The atmosphere acts as a thermo blanket because it:
options: Maintains a specific temperature for organisms on earth
Reflects all sunlight back to space
mcqs.why: The atmosphere serves as a thermo blanket which maintains a specific temperature for organisms. It also protects the earth and life from the hazardous radiation of space.

mcqs.q: Water vapours form about what part of the atmosphere?
mcqs.why: About 1% water vapours are also an important part of the atmosphere, alongside 78% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Why must the composition of the atmosphere be maintained as it is?
options: Because gases cannot be replaced once lost
Because the atmosphere has a solid boundary
Because oxygen is produced only by animals
Any change in composition could be fatal to all life forms
mcqs.why: The constituents are present in different layers, each having a distinct character. Any change in composition could be fatal to all life forms, so it must be maintained as it is.

mcqs.q: All living things rely on air mainly for:
mcqs.why: All living things rely on air for normal life processes, e.g. respiration. The atmosphere also works as a thermo blanket and a protective shield.

mcqs.q: The atmosphere protects the earth and life from:
mcqs.why: Its coating of gases protects the earth and life from the hazardous radiation of space, especially through layers such as the ozone-containing stratosphere.

lessons.title: 14.2 The Layers of Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
The Layers of the Atmosphere

The atmosphere is made up of several layers, composed of different constituents, and each layer serves in a different way.

LayerExtentMain Features
TroposphereSurface to 7-14 kmLowest layer; about 75% of atmospheric mass
StratosphereUp to about 50 kmContains the ozone layer
MesosphereAbout 50 km to 90 kmColdest region; 20 C to -80 C
ThermosphereClosest to spaceHuge solar energy, but atoms far apart

Troposphere and Stratosphere

  • The troposphere is the only layer that can support life. Large amounts of water vapour are present, clouds develop here and birds fly here.
  • The stratosphere begins at the tropopause. Its importance is the ozone layer (ozonosphere), where ozone (O3), an allotropic form of oxygen, absorbs UV radiation. The energy is radiated as IR, heating this layer.
  • Without ozone, UV radiations would flood the earth and destroy life.

Mesosphere and Thermosphere

  • In the mesosphere, temperature falls as we move upward. Oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide amounts are almost the same as near the surface, water vapour is very low, and meteors burn up here, seen as shooting stars.
  • The thermosphere has huge energy from solar radiations, but atoms are few and far apart, so heat transfer is too low and overall heat remains low and harmless.

Key Points

  • Four layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.
  • Troposphere (7-14 km) holds about 75% of the mass and is the only life-supporting layer.
  • Stratosphere extends to about 50 km and contains the protective ozone layer.
  • Mesosphere (50-90 km) is the coldest layer, from 20 C to -80 C; meteors burn up in it.
  • Thermosphere is closest to space; its overall heat remains low despite huge energy.

mcqs.q: The troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere, extends from the surface to:
options: 7-14 km, and holds about 75% of the atmospheric mass
mcqs.why: Troposphere: surface to 7-14 km, the lowest layer with about 75% of atmospheric mass. The stratosphere reaches up to about 50 km and the mesosphere from about 50 to 90 km.

mcqs.q: The ozone layer is present in the:
options: Stratosphere, which extends up to about 50 km
mcqs.why: The stratosphere contains the ozone layer (ozonosphere), where ozone O3, an allotropic form of oxygen, absorbs UV radiation and the energy is radiated as IR, heating this layer.

mcqs.q: The only layer of the atmosphere that can support life is the:
mcqs.why: The troposphere is the only layer that can support life. Large amounts of water vapour are present, clouds develop here and birds fly here.

mcqs.q: The mesosphere (about 50 km to 90 km) is known for being:
options: The coldest region, with temperature from 20 C down to -80 C, where meteors burn up
The warmest layer of the atmosphere
The layer containing the ozone layer
The layer where clouds are formed
mcqs.why: Mesosphere: about 50 km to 90 km, the coldest region, 20 C to -80 C; temperature falls as we move upward and meteors burn up here, seen as shooting stars.

mcqs.q: In the thermosphere, the overall heat remains low despite huge solar energy because:
options: There is no solar energy in this layer
The atoms are few and far apart, so heat transfer is too low
The layer is filled with ice crystals
mcqs.why: The thermosphere is closest to space and has huge energy from solar radiations, but atoms are few and far apart, so heat transfer is too low and overall heat remains low and harmless.

mcqs.q: Ozone, O3, is an allotropic form of:
mcqs.why: Ozone (O3) is an allotropic form of oxygen present in the stratosphere, where it absorbs UV radiation. Without ozone, UV radiations would flood the earth and destroy life.

mcqs.q: The boundary where the stratosphere begins is called the:
mcqs.why: The stratosphere begins at the tropopause, the top of the troposphere. Its importance is the ozone layer, which protects life from UV radiation.

mcqs.q: Clouds develop and birds fly in which layer?
mcqs.why: In the troposphere, large amounts of water vapour are present, clouds develop here and birds fly here. It is also the only life-supporting layer.

mcqs.q: Meteors burn up in the mesosphere and are seen as:
mcqs.why: In the mesosphere, meteors burn up and are seen as shooting stars. Water vapour is very low there, while oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide amounts are almost the same as near the surface.

mcqs.q: If there were no ozone layer, ultraviolet radiations would:
options: Flood the earth and destroy life
Have no effect on living things
mcqs.why: Without ozone, UV radiations would flood the earth and destroy life. Ozone absorbs UV and the energy is radiated as IR, heating the stratosphere.

lessons.title: 14.3 Environmental Pollution and Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Pollution and Pollutants

A pollutant is a substance that contaminates the earth's environment, affecting quality of life or the natural functioning of ecosystems. Its coming into the environment is environmental pollution. Some is natural (volcanic eruptions); most is caused by human activities.

  • Biodegradable pollutants: decompose rapidly by natural processes, e.g. sewage, CO, CO2, SO2, NO, NO2. A problem when added faster than they decompose.
  • Non-degradable pollutants: do not decompose, or decompose slowly, e.g. CFCs, dioxin pesticides, plastics, radioactive materials; difficult or impossible to remove.

Types: air pollution, water pollution, soil contamination, noise pollution, visual pollution. This chapter deals with air pollution from industry and motor vehicles.

Major Air Pollutants

  • Primary pollutants pollute directly: SO2, NOx, COx, hydrocarbons, dust, ash, smoke.
  • Secondary pollutants pollute indirectly, produced by primary pollutants: ground level ozone, smog (smoke + fog, severe in winter).
  • SO2: burning coal/oil containing sulphur; causes acid rain. NO2: high temperature combustion; also acid rain.
  • CO: incomplete combustion of natural gas, coal or wood; vehicular exhaust is a major source.
  • CO2: emitted in combustion; causes the greenhouse effect (increase in temperature of the earth's atmosphere).
  • Particulates: smoke, dust, poisonous lead; 2.5-10 micrometers, enter nasal cavity, bronchia and lungs.
  • CFCs: contain Cl and F; from spray paints, Freon refrigerant, DDT; harmful to the ozone layer.
  • Others: radioactive pollutants (nuclear explosions, hospitals), ground level ozone (poisonous; high-voltage equipment), odours (garbage, sewage).

Key Points

  • A pollutant contaminates the environment; its entry is environmental pollution.
  • Biodegradable pollutants decompose rapidly; non-degradable ones like CFCs and plastics do not.
  • Primary pollutants act directly; secondary pollutants like smog act indirectly.
  • SO2 and NO2 cause acid rain; CO2 causes the greenhouse effect; CFCs harm ozone.

mcqs.q: A pollutant is defined as:
options: Any gas present in the atmosphere
A substance that is useful for plants
A substance that contaminates the earth's environment, affecting quality of life or the natural functioning of ecosystems
Any substance found in sea water
mcqs.why: A pollutant is a substance that contaminates the earth's environment, affecting quality of life or the natural functioning of ecosystems; its coming into the environment is environmental pollution.

mcqs.q: Biodegradable pollutants, e.g. sewage, CO, CO2, SO2, NO and NO2, are those which:
options: Are always harmless in any amount
Decompose rapidly by natural processes, but become a problem when added faster than they decompose
mcqs.why: Biodegradable pollutants decompose rapidly by natural processes, e.g. sewage, CO, CO2, SO2, NO, NO2. They become a problem when added faster than they decompose.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-degradable pollutant?
mcqs.why: Non-degradable pollutants do not decompose, or decompose slowly, e.g. CFCs, dioxin pesticides, plastics and radioactive materials; they are difficult or impossible to remove.

mcqs.q: Primary pollutants pollute directly; an example set is:
options: SO2, NOx, COx, hydrocarbons, dust, ash and smoke
mcqs.why: Primary pollutants pollute directly: SO2, NOx, COx, hydrocarbons, dust, ash, smoke. Secondary pollutants pollute indirectly and are produced by primary pollutants, e.g. ground level ozone and smog.

mcqs.q: Smog, a secondary pollutant, is a mixture of:
options: Smoke and fog, and it is severe in winter
mcqs.why: Secondary pollutants include ground level ozone and smog (smoke + fog), which is severe in winter. Smog is produced indirectly from primary pollutants.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is caused mainly by which pair of air pollutants?
options: SO2 (from burning coal/oil containing sulphur) and NO2 (from high temperature combustion)
mcqs.why: SO2 comes from burning coal/oil containing sulphur and causes acid rain; NO2 from high temperature combustion also causes acid rain. CO2 instead causes the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide, CO, is produced by:
options: Incomplete combustion of natural gas, coal or wood; vehicular exhaust is a major source
mcqs.why: CO is produced by incomplete combustion of natural gas, coal or wood; vehicular exhaust is a major source. Complete combustion produces CO2 instead.

mcqs.q: The greenhouse effect, an increase in the temperature of the earth's atmosphere, is caused by:
options: Carbon dioxide, CO2, emitted in combustion
mcqs.why: CO2 is emitted in combustion and causes the greenhouse effect (increase in temperature of the earth's atmosphere). SO2 and NO2 cause acid rain, and CFCs harm the ozone layer.

mcqs.q: Particulates such as smoke, dust and poisonous lead are harmful because their size of 2.5-10 micrometers lets them:
options: Enter the nasal cavity, bronchia and lungs
mcqs.why: Particulates: smoke, dust, poisonous lead; 2.5-10 micrometers, so they enter the nasal cavity, bronchia and lungs and damage health.

mcqs.q: CFCs, which harm the ozone layer, come from:
options: Spray paints, Freon refrigerant and DDT; they contain chlorine and fluorine
mcqs.why: CFCs contain Cl and F and come from spray paints, Freon refrigerant and DDT; they are harmful to the ozone layer. Some pollution is natural, e.g. volcanic eruptions, but most is caused by human activities.

lessons.title: 14.4 The Acid Rain and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
What is Acid Rain?

Acid rain is rainfall that has a pH level of less than 5.6. It is caused chiefly by two types of oxides: sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides. These oxides combine with moisture in the atmosphere to make sulphuric acid and nitric acid.

Formation of Acid Rain

  • Sulphur dioxide reacts with the oxygen of air to give SO3, which combines with water to form sulphuric acid:

2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)

SO3(g) + H2O(l) -> H2SO4(aq)

  • Oxides of nitrogen combine with water of the atmosphere to form acidic products:

2NO2(g) + H2O(l) -> HNO3(aq) + HNO2(aq)

These acids can be carried far from their origin in clouds and then come down as rainfall.

Effects of Acid Rain

  • It directly destroys the life forms where it falls.
  • It has adverse impacts on forests, freshwaters and soils.
  • It kills off insect and aquatic life forms.
  • It causes damage to buildings and has possible impacts on human health.

To prevent acid rains, international treaties (e.g. Montreal and Kyoto treaties) on the long-range transport of atmospheric pollutants have been agreed, which have significantly reduced the emission of hazardous gases and thus cut down acid rains.

Key Points

  • Acid rain is rainfall with pH less than 5.6.
  • It is formed when sulphur and nitrogen oxides combine with atmospheric moisture to form H2SO4 and HNO3.
  • It damages forests, freshwaters, soils, buildings, aquatic life and human health.
  • Montreal and Kyoto treaties have reduced hazardous gas emissions and acid rains.

mcqs.q: Acid rain is rainfall that has a pH level of:
mcqs.why: Acid rain is rainfall that has a pH level of less than 5.6. It is caused chiefly by sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides combining with atmospheric moisture.

mcqs.q: The two types of oxides chiefly responsible for acid rain are:
mcqs.why: Acid rain is caused chiefly by two types of oxides: sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides. These oxides combine with moisture in the atmosphere to make sulphuric acid and nitric acid.

mcqs.q: The first step in the formation of sulphuric acid in acid rain is:
mcqs.why: Sulphur dioxide reacts with the oxygen of air to give SO3: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3. The SO3 then combines with water to form sulphuric acid, H2SO4.

mcqs.q: Sulphur trioxide forms sulphuric acid by reacting with water:
mcqs.why: SO3(g) + H2O(l) -> H2SO4(aq). Together with 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3, this is how sulphur oxides turn into the sulphuric acid of acid rain.

mcqs.q: Oxides of nitrogen combine with atmospheric water to form:
mcqs.why: Oxides of nitrogen combine with water of the atmosphere to form acidic products: 2NO2(g) + H2O(l) -> HNO3(aq) + HNO2(aq), nitric acid and nitrous acid.

mcqs.q: The acids formed in the atmosphere can reach the ground far from their origin because they:
options: Are carried far from their origin in clouds and then come down as rainfall
mcqs.why: These acids can be carried far from their origin in clouds and then come down as rainfall, so acid rain can damage areas far away from the industries that produced the gases.

mcqs.q: Which is an effect of acid rain?
options: It increases the fertility of all soils
It damages forests, freshwaters and soils, and kills insect and aquatic life forms
mcqs.why: Acid rain directly destroys the life forms where it falls, has adverse impacts on forests, freshwaters and soils, kills off insect and aquatic life forms, and damages buildings and human health.

mcqs.q: International treaties that have reduced hazardous gas emissions and thus cut down acid rains include:
options: The Geneva and Vienna conventions only
The Paris and London agreements only
No treaty has ever addressed acid rain
mcqs.why: To prevent acid rains, international treaties (e.g. Montreal and Kyoto treaties) on the long-range transport of atmospheric pollutants have been agreed, significantly reducing emissions of hazardous gases.

mcqs.q: Acid rain damages buildings mainly because:
options: The rain is heavier than normal rain
The rain contains solid dust particles
The rain falls only at night
The acids in the rain attack the building materials
mcqs.why: Acid rain causes damage to buildings and has possible impacts on human health, because the sulphuric and nitric acids formed in the air react with and corrode building materials.

mcqs.q: The pH of acid rain is compared against normal rain: acid rain has pH:
options: Below 5.6, because dissolved sulphur and nitrogen oxides make it acidic
mcqs.why: Acid rain is rainfall with pH less than 5.6. The oxides SO2/SO3 and NO2 dissolve in moisture to give H2SO4, HNO3 and HNO2, lowering the pH.

lessons.title: 14.5 Ozone Depletion and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
The Protective Ozone Layer

A protective layer of ozone gas is present in the upper atmosphere (stratosphere), which protects the earth from highly energetic and dangerous ultraviolet radiations:

O3(g) + uv -> O(g) + O2(g)

The O2 produced again combines with the atomic oxygen to yield the ozone back:

O2(g) + O(g) -> O3(g)

How CFCs Deplete Ozone

In the late 1970s, scientists found that chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage this protective layer. Chlorine from CFCs reacts with ozone in a chain reaction:

Cl(g) + O3(g) -> ClO(g) + O2(g)

O3(g) -> O(g) + O2(g) (in UV light)

ClO(g) + O(g) -> Cl(g) + O2(g)

This is a chain reaction: a single chlorine atom depletes thousands of ozone molecules, so ozone is constantly depleting.

Effects of Ozone Depletion

  • More UV radiation reaches the earth's surface, which is expected to increase skin cancer in humans.
  • Increased UV radiations destroy micro-organisms, thus imbalancing the entire ecosystem.
  • The increase in UV also causes global warming directly and indirectly.
  • The ozone hole so far discovered is at the Antarctic region, where life is not so abundant, so damage to life has not yet been caused by this hole, but measures are required to stop this damage.
  • An important step taken is the ban on the usage of CFCs.

Note: ozone itself is poisonous at ground level, where sparks in electric equipment produce it; ground level ozone is a form of air pollution.

Key Points

  • Ozone in the stratosphere protects the earth from dangerous UV radiations.
  • Ozone is formed back by O2 + O -> O3, keeping a natural cycle.
  • CFCs release chlorine, and one chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction.
  • Ozone depletion increases skin cancer, destroys micro-organisms and causes global warming.
  • The ozone hole is over the Antarctic region; banning CFCs is the key protective step.

mcqs.q: The ozone layer protects the earth from:
options: Highly energetic and dangerous ultraviolet radiations
mcqs.why: A protective layer of ozone gas is present in the upper atmosphere (stratosphere), which protects the earth from highly energetic and dangerous ultraviolet radiations: O3 + uv -> O + O2.

mcqs.q: Ozone is re-formed in the stratosphere by the reaction:
mcqs.why: The O2 produced again combines with the atomic oxygen to yield the ozone back: O2(g) + O(g) -> O3(g). This keeps a natural cycle of ozone formation and breakdown.

mcqs.q: Scientists found in the late 1970s that the chemicals damaging the ozone layer are:
mcqs.why: In the late 1970s, scientists found that chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the protective ozone layer. Chlorine from CFCs reacts with ozone in a chain reaction.

mcqs.q: In the first step of ozone destruction by chlorine:
mcqs.why: Chlorine from CFCs reacts with ozone: Cl(g) + O3(g) -> ClO(g) + O2(g). Then ClO reacts with atomic oxygen to regenerate Cl, so the chain continues.

mcqs.q: The reaction ClO(g) + O(g) -> Cl(g) + O2(g) is dangerous because it:
options: Regenerates the chlorine atom, so one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction
Consumes all the chlorine at once
mcqs.why: This is a chain reaction: ClO + O gives back Cl + O2, so a single chlorine atom depletes thousands of ozone molecules and ozone is constantly depleting.

mcqs.q: Ozone depletion is expected to increase which disease in humans?
options: Skin cancer, because more UV radiation reaches the earth's surface
mcqs.why: More UV radiation reaches the earth's surface due to ozone depletion, which is expected to increase skin cancer in humans. Increased UV also destroys micro-organisms, imbalancing the ecosystem.

mcqs.q: Increased UV radiation due to ozone depletion also harms the ecosystem by:
options: Increasing the growth of all plants
Destroying micro-organisms, thus imbalancing the entire ecosystem, and causing global warming directly and indirectly
Reducing the temperature of the earth

mcqs.why: The ozone hole so far discovered is at the Antarctic region, where life is not so abundant, so damage to life has not yet been caused by this hole, but measures are required to stop this damage.

lessons.title: 15.1 Water and Properties of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Water on Earth

Water is an essential part of all living forms. The water of the Earth is called the hydrosphere. It is used on a large scale for drinking, washing and cultivation, yet the water actually available to humans is limited, so water scarcity is common in most areas.

Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface.

PartShare
Salt water (oceans and ground saline water)97.5%
Fresh water2.5%
Fresh water in glaciers and polar ice caps68.7% of fresh water
Ground water30.1% of fresh water
Surface water1.2% of fresh water
Water available for our useabout 0.7% of total water

The Water Cycle

Water moves perpetually through the water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off, usually reaching the sea. Humans have disturbed this cycle for centuries, more so with industrialization.

Properties of Water (15.1.1)

Pure water, H2O, is colourless and tasteless.

  • At normal temperature and pressure it is a liquid.
  • It is a neutral compound; it shows no acidic or basic properties.
  • It dissolves many inorganic and organic substances.
  • Ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on the sea and life underneath continues to grow.
  • It has a high heat capacity, 4.18 Jg-1 C-1. It absorbs heat in the day, so the Earth's temperature does not fall too low at night.

Key Points

  • Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface; 97.5% is salt water and only 2.5% is fresh water.
  • Only about 0.7% of the total water is available for human use.
  • The water cycle works by evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off.
  • Pure water is colourless, tasteless and neutral, with formula H2O.
  • Ice is less dense than water, so it floats; water has a high heat capacity of 4.18 Jg-1 C-1.

mcqs.why: Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface. Of all this water, 97.5% is salt water and only 2.5% is fresh water.

mcqs.why: Salt water is 97.5% and fresh water is 2.5% of the total. Of the fresh water, 68.7% is in glaciers and polar ice caps, 30.1% is ground water and 1.2% is surface water.

mcqs.why: Working: fresh water is 2.5% of the total, so in 1,000 kg there is 2.5/100 x 1,000 = 25 kg of fresh water (and 975 kg of salt water).

mcqs.why: Fresh water in glaciers and polar ice caps is 68.7% of fresh water; ground water is 30.1% and surface water only 1.2% of fresh water.

mcqs.why: Water available for our use is about 0.7% of total water, which is why water scarcity is common in most areas despite water covering 71% of the surface.

options: Evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off, usually reaching the sea
mcqs.why: Water moves perpetually through the water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, precipitation and run-off, usually reaching the sea. Humans have disturbed this cycle, more so with industrialization.

mcqs.why: Pure water, H2O, is colourless and tasteless. At normal temperature and pressure it is a liquid, it is neutral (no acidic or basic properties) and it dissolves many inorganic and organic substances.

options: Ice is heavier than liquid water
Sea water pushes the ice upward
Ice is less dense than liquid water
mcqs.why: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats on the sea and life underneath continues to grow. This is one of the special properties of water.

mcqs.q: The heat capacity of water is 4.18 J/g/C. The heat needed to raise the temperature of 10 g of water by 1 C is:
mcqs.why: Working: heat = heat capacity x mass x temperature rise = 4.18 x 10 x 1 = 41.8 J. Water's high heat capacity means it absorbs heat in the day, so the Earth's temperature does not fall too low at night.

mcqs.q: The water of the Earth as a whole is called the:
mcqs.why: Water is an essential part of all living forms. The water of the Earth is called the hydrosphere, used on a large scale for drinking, washing and cultivation.

lessons.title: 15.2 Water as a Solvent
lessons.notes_html:
An Excellent Solvent

Water as a solvent: water is an excellent solvent. It dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds.

Structure of Water

  • Water is made of two kinds of atoms: oxygen and hydrogen.
  • The angle between the H-O-H atoms is 104.45 degrees.
  • The O-H distance is 0.9584 A.
  • Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C.

Why Water Dissolves So Much

This high solubility is due to the polar nature of water. The shared electrons are attracted towards the central oxygen, so oxygen carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge.

When a substance dissolves, the negative part of the solute is captured by the positive part of water, and the positive part of the solute is attracted by the negative part of water. The solute particles are thus dissolved. This process is called solvation.

In the solvation of table salt, NaCl, the polar substance breaks up into ions. The ions are masked by water molecules through their poles, and new forces develop in this solute-solvent interaction.

Key Points

  • Water dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds.
  • The H-O-H angle is 104.45 degrees and the O-H distance is 0.9584 A.
  • Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C.
  • Water is polar: oxygen is partly negative and hydrogen is partly positive.
  • Solvation is the process in which water molecules surround the parts or ions of a solute and dissolve it, as with NaCl.

options: Dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds
mcqs.why: Water is an excellent solvent: it dissolves most inorganic and many organic compounds, because of its polar nature.

mcqs.why: The angle between the H-O-H atoms is 104.45 degrees and the O-H distance is 0.9584 A. (The 109.5 degree angle belongs to tetrahedral methane.)

mcqs.why: The O-H distance is 0.9584 A and the H-O-H angle is 104.45 degrees. Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C.

mcqs.why: Pure water boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C at normal pressure. Its molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

options: It contains equal numbers of protons and neutrons
The shared electrons are attracted towards the central oxygen, so oxygen carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge
mcqs.why: This high solubility is due to the polar nature of water: oxygen carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge, so water attracts both parts of a solute.

Water molecules surround the parts or ions of a solute and dissolve it
mcqs.why: In solvation, the negative part of the solute is captured by the positive part of water and the positive part by the negative part of water, so the solute particles are dissolved.

mcqs.why: In the solvation of table salt, NaCl, the polar substance breaks up into ions. The ions are masked by water molecules through their poles, and new forces develop in this solute-solvent interaction.

mcqs.why: The shared electrons are attracted towards the central oxygen, so oxygen carries a partial negative charge and each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge — the basis of water's solvent action.

mcqs.why: Water is made of two kinds of atoms: oxygen and hydrogen, in the ratio 2:1, giving H2O with an H-O-H angle of 104.45 degrees.
